subtopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS-DIVISION AFTER A RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, With your permission I would like to ask the attention of the House for a moment to what might be called a question of privilege, I suppose, though it does not concern me any more than any other member of the House. It is to a telegram from Ottawa in the Montreal Gazette of Wednesday concerning the division of the previous evening. The correspondent writes:
It has been an unwritten rule of Parliament since confederation that there would be no vote on the day following a recess. This was an amenity of Parliament that has never been violated until to-day by the new Liberal leader.

I believe, Sir, I have to plead guilty to being now one of the oldest members of Parliament. I think there are only two, possibly three, who were here before me. With about twenty years of experience, I want to say that I have never heard of such a rule. I have consulted a number of the older members of the House, each one of whom tells me that he never heard of such a rule. It is quite evident, therefore, that the Gazette correspondent was misinformed and mislead.

Trade and Commerce-bounties on crude *petroleum, administration of the Act, $3,000.

Before you proceed
with this item, Sir, the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) said last night that he intended to proceed with the Estimates of the Labour Department to-day. The Estimates of that department have not been taken up previously, and I will object to their being proceeded with to-day. Before we proceed with the estimates of the Labour Department, I have a few remarks to make about the hon. gentleman who presides over that department and about certain matters concerning it.

I have been using a copy
of the Estimates printed in French. I have no copy of the Estimates in English, and I object to proceeding with the Estimates unless we have English copies.

Does the hon.
member object to the committee proceeding with the Estimates because he has not a copy of them in hand? These Estimates were printed as usual and a copy was placed in the box of every member weeks ago. My hon. friend has allowed his copy to drop out of his pocket. He must not



hold us all up because he has happened to lose his copy.

I stated that I have only a French copy of the Estimates; I have not an English copy, and I do not think it is an answer to say that the Estimates have been distributed once. My objection can be withdrawn, but we will discuss these Estimates in French, and I want to know if the Government is willing to proceed on that understanding.

In support of my hon.
friend's contention, last week I applied for a copy of the Estimates in English, and I was told by the distribution office that they had none in hand. I hold here a copy of the Estimates in French. I have no objection whatsoever to holding a French copy; it suits me better to discuss the Estimates in French than it would to discuss them in English; but on the other hand, as my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) has said, as we have in our possession only copies of the Estimates in French, it would be only reasonable and natural that we should carry on the discussion in the language in which the Estimates are printed.

The minister speaks in
French now. We can proceed.
What does the term "administration of the Act'' mean in this case?

This appropriation has been passed every year for a long series of years. The object is to pay the salary and expenses of the officer or officers supervising the payment of the bounty upon crude petroleum oil. That bounty is granted, of course, by Act of Parliament; it has to be paid out under the regulations of the department, and the $3,000 is to pay for the supervisor and his aids, and for contingencies and travelling expenses. The work of the supervisor fs to see that all claims that are made for payment of bounty are correct, to compare them and to issue his certificate as to their payment.
What amount of bounties has been paid? Or are any bounties being paid?

The bounties
paid for the fiscal year 1918-19 on crude petroleum oil amounted to $162,187; for 1919-20, to $103,753; and for 1920-21 up to January 31, to $70,908.

WThat people were the
bounties paid to?

To the producers of the oil in two or three counties in Ontario where petroleum is produced; in New Brunswick where some oil is produced from the shales; and in Alberta where some oil coming under this Act is produced. The main part is paid to producers of oil in some two or three Ontario counties.

(Translation.) Are those grants paid by the Government simply to individual owners of oil wells, or are they also paid to corporations and companies, say, for instance, the Imperial Oil and other trusts, which sell the oil at such a high price?
I must ask my hon. friend to speak a little louder and a little more distinctly, and especially to couch his question in particularly good French, so that it will commend itself to my ear.
I am quite sure-
That is better.

I am quite sure my right hon. friend is too modest. He has taken part in several conferences overseas; he has represented Canada with much honour and dignity at the Peace Conference; he has also represented our country at Geneva; and last year at the opening of Parliament, much to the pleasure and appreciation of hon. members on this side of the House, acting as Prime Minister of our country he delivered a magnificent, able, and, as usual, very eloquent speech in the French language. I am quite sure my right hon. friend understands French just as well as I do, and I a*n inclined to think he speaks French even better than I can speak it myself. But for the convenience, not of my right hon. friend who is a very noted bi-linguist, but of other members who might not be so conversant with the French language, I will proceed in English. I do not do so, however, for the convenience of my right hon. friend because I am sure he could carry on the discussion in French. The question I put to the minister is this: Are those premiums paid by the Government simply to individual owners of petroleum wells, or are they also paid to corporations and companies, say, for instance, the Imperial Oil and those very large trust companies which sell the oil at such a high price that I do not see why we give them premiums at all?
The premiums are paid in all cases to the people who produce the oil.	*
Are any premiums paid to corporations or companies?
I think not.

The right hon. gentleman says he thinks not. I would like to be sure on that point. As far as I am concerned, I do not think this House ought to pay a cent of bounty to any corporation like the Imperial Oil, and before we proceed any further with this item I would like the minister to make sure whether premiums are paid to this corporation. If they are being paid, I think he ought to see to it that they are not paid in future. This Government is not rich enough to give money to the Imperial Oil Company, the Standard Oil Company, or Rockefeller. We have heavy enough financial obligations to meet without throwing away our money to people who are richer than the Government itself.

If I might be allowed to interfere, at the expense of my hon. friend's well-turned and eloquent periods, I will give him the information absolutely that the bounties are paid only to those who produce the oil, so neither Rockefeller nor the Imperial Oil Company gets a squint at it.

It does not seem to me to be of essential difference whether this bounty is paid to a large company or to a small operator. I wish to state to the committee, and I think that what I say will have a responsive echo in the country, if not in the House, that for the Government to bonus an industry which is able to sell its products at the prices at which coal oil products are selling now is, in view of the present financial condition of the country, most unwise, to use the most modest term.
Can't you make it a little stronger? .
I would say it was rank, raging lunacy, to' speak plainly. In view of the respect which I have for the minister I couched my language in the most modest and gentle terms.

In the interests of my hon. friend himself will he allow me to intervene for a moment? I have noted the hard language which he has applied to this policy of bonusing. Does my hon. friend know that that policy was inaugurated in 1904, that it was re-inaugurated in 1907 and 1908, that it is there on the statute books by virtue of the con-
884 '
centrated wisdom of the Liberal Government to which my hon. friend paid allegiance, and which he considers to be one of the finest Governments that ever existed, in Canada? It is ungrateful of my hon. friend after all the prominence that his party has given to it to stand up behind his aged and revered leader (Mr. Fielding) and tax him with introducing a policy of rank and unadulterated lunacy.

I have listened to the defence of this policy of bonusing by probably the ablest man on the opposite side of the House, and it has taken the form of chiding me because the Liberal party, when I was not in the House, did something which I trust I would have opposed then as I oppose it now.
But you sacrificed at their altars then.

I have this to say. I have always been against bonusing, I have always been against protection; I think it is a mistake, and that it was a mistake when it was brought about by the party to which I gave my allegiance at that time, and to which I give my allegiance now. I would, however, make this observation, and I believe the minister will consider it reasonable, that when the public debt of Canada was between $250,000,000 and $300,000,000 there was more excuse

I do not say more reason-
In principle?

There was more excuse for the giving of bonuses then, than there is at a time when, as I am sure the minister will agree, the financial condition of this country is a very serious one indeed. I hope that the minister will see his way clear, even if it is necessary to bring down legislation for that purpose to stop bonusing this industry, which I do not believe requires bonusing. If it has been bonused since 1904, it is about time it stood on its own feet, about time that the cask of petroleum stood on its own bottom. I protest energetically against what I consider to be this waste of public funds. I protests against the giving of bonuses by a country in the financial condition in which we find ourselves to-day.

I am only
administering the Act.
I should like to ask the minister how he reconciles the policy of bunusing oil production with the policy of collecting royalties on oil production, as we have it in the West?

If my Ron. friend or others are interested in looking at the history of this particular transaction, they will fin'd, I think, that the bonus was given to the oil producers at the time when the duty was taken off crude potroleum entering this country from the United States and other contries. When petroleum was made free, on the theory that it would be of great general benefit, it was felt by those who were administering the aifairs of the country at that time that the producers of oil should he compensated for this introduction of free petroleum-That was the theory on which the bounty was paid.

I asked the minister whether large corporations like the Imperial Oil were getting any of these bounties, and he answered that he thought they were not. He was not very explicit in his answer. He did not say that no public moneys were being given to these very large corporations, these trusts which are crushing the people of Canada, and to which we should not give a cent.

I think my hon. friend must be wrong with reference to my assertion. I think I told him that the bounties were given simply to the producers of oil, and not to companies who do not produce or raise the oil.
But suppose the Imperial Oil Company is the producer of oil on certain lands. Would they get a bonus for producing oil? That is what I want to know.
The Act, of course, provides how the money shall be paid. The provision, as I find it here-

I understand the
minister is about to tell the committee how the payments are made, but that is not the information I want; we can come to that later. I want to know whether the Imperial Oil Company, if it produces oil on lands in Canada, is entitled to this bounty. Should the Government pay premiums to the Imperial Oil Company?

I will read the section of the Act to my hon. friend, who I believe is a lawyer:
The sai-d bounty to be paid to or divided among the producers of the petroleum, the owner or occupier of the soil through which it is mined or won, or such other person interested, or injuriously affected by the mining operations or works as the Governor i-n Council by regulation approves.
I think that explains, it.
If I understand the minister rightly, that means that the Imperial Oil Company occupy, own, or lease land upon which oil is produced. Then they would receive a bounty from the Government?
Being a producer, they would, I suppose.
The minister says they would. I want to know, has the Imperial Oil Company, as a fact, received a bounty?

Now my hon. friend asks a question as to a specific point. I have not the information, but my own impression is that tne vast majority of the bounty is paid to the small producers of oil throughout the different districts. I am not prepared to say that there is not a company producing oil in those districts and that no such company is getting the bounty upon what it produces.

Now I desire to call the attention of the committee to this point: About ten days ago my hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) complained that we had not sufficient information to enable us to discuss the Estimates intelligently. The Prime Minister's attention was drawn to the fact that the fourth volume of the Auditor General's report had not been brought down yet, and that therefore the members on this side as well as hon. gentlemen opposite could not possibly consider the Estimates with that degree of care and scrutiny which is only proper. In reply to that representation, the right hon. gentleman who leads the House gave the formal and definite assurance that no items would be discussed unless information in connection therewith were first available to hon. members. If my right hon. friend refers to page 2 of the index of volume III of the Auditor General's report he will find therein stated that details in connection with crude petroleum are to be fomrn under " Z-23 Now, " Z-23 " is not in our hands; it is in the fourth volume. In view of the assurance given us by the Prime Minister I would ask my right hon. friend to postpone this item.
Item stands.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Sir George Foster moves that further consideration of item 346 be postponed.
Mr. Chairman, before we leave this item-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am very sorry, but the motion to postpone consideration of an item is not debatable.
Item stands.
Bounty on Linen Yarn spun in Canada from Canadian Flax, including expenses of supervision,' under Order in Council of September 3, 1918, $26,000.

I desire some information regarding this item, in view of the present condition of the flax market in Canada, and also in view of some letters I have received regarding the loss already sustained and the further loss which is anticipated by those who have produced flax, particularly in western Ontario. I am in formed that the flax men throughout that part of the Dominion stand to be ruined one after another by the decline in the prevailing prices, whicn have fallen con siderably since last year. I cannot give the prices in detail except as regards seea, which I understand was a year ago $6 a bushel and now has dropped $1.50. I have a communication from certain men wh>. say that they stand to be ruined by the; conditions under which they have to work. Now, I notice that the item this year is being reduced by the sum of $4,000. If the principle is a sound one of assisting, by way of bonus, the manufacture of lipen, I think this is a most inopportune time in the history of the country to make any reduction in this grant. On the contrary, I think it ought to be increased. Is the minister or his department seized of the extreme distress in trade that now exists and is likely to be aggravated by the failure of the flax producers to dispose either of their fibre or of their seed? If the matter has been brought to the attention of the Government or of the minister, I snould like to know what activities are in progress in the department to ameliorate the very serious conditions which have overtaken the flax interests, as a direct outcome, I fancy, of the war.

The department over which I preside has had numerous communications from flax growers, par-ticlurly in the province of Ontario, regarding the difficulties under which they are labouring at the present time, difficulties which are summed up in the fact stated by my hon. friend, that the prices for either fibre or seed have very suddenly and largely dropped from those that prevailed a year or two ago. The hon. gentleman very properly said that he supposed this resulted from the general war conditions.
It is a disability being suffered not only by flax producers but also, more or less, by the producers of very many of the staple articles of the country. For instance, I see that July wheat is selling on the Chicago market to-day at $1.25, which is a great come-down fro mthe price of $2.08 to $3.00 per bushel which prevailed on the market a year or so ago. The Department of Trade and Commerce cannot, of course, undertake to keep up prices nor to remunerate producers who have on hand stocks which they cannot get rid of at former prices and which consequently they must sell at a loss. But it is working in conjunction with these producers in an endeavour to find as profitable markets as possible in the different parts of the foreign field, and our trade commissioners are specially charged at the present time with this matter, being in possession of information which has been supplied me by the flax growers themselves. I do not know what will be the outcome. I am afraid there is not very much hope that these products, either fibre or seed, will regain anything like the values which they have had in the preceding three or four years. The special item under consideration is not intended as a relief to producers of flax. It is a child of the war, and the action which resulted in this bounty being granted for a period of three years was a direct outcome of the necessities of the war. At a certain time Canada found herself unable to get linen thread or yarn, either from the United States or from Great Britain, and this article was called for from all parts of the country for use by fishermen as well as for manufacturing purposes of various kinds. The War Commission, which was functioning at that time, took the matter up on the suggestion of Council, and in the end an Order in Council was passed by which it was proposed to give a bounty for the manufacture of linen thread and yarns of certain sizes, the bounty to be payable for three years after the Peace Treaty had been put into force, but not to be payable to the manufacturers of these yarns until the war had ended. The theory was that if manufacturers installed the equipment necessary for the production of these yarns, which had not before been made in Canada, the prices which could be charged for them, owing to the scarcity of the article, would be sufficient remuneration for the time that the war lasted, but-as this was an unusual and an emergent thing-when the war was

over, and supplies were available in greater quantity, the prices would tend to recede. Then the bounty was to take effect, and be paid according to the scale agreed upon, for three years after the war had ended. Some manufacturers undertook to equip their factories; but only one has really provided the required equipment, the owner, I think, of a factory at Guelph. That factory is now not only making linen yarns out of the Canadian product, but is also turning-out a superior quality of linen goods of the coarser and of the finer kinds as well.
I have seen an exhibition of these goods- either in Ottawa or in some other city-[DOT] and they certainly are of excellent make; the quality of the fibre and the finish of the product seems to be everything that can be asked. To the extent that they manufacture, they may avail themselves of the bounty as given on these yarns up to the maximum; but in no year may the bounty paid to all manufacturers of yarns exceed $25,000, nor is it in the three years to exceed the sum of $75,000. The vote asked for here is for the purpose of paying the bounty as agreed upon, and as I have explained to the committee. The sum is smaller than was estimated for previously, and even the amount of this estimate may be reduced somewhat-in fact I am going to ask that it be reduced-simply because it is impossible for the manufacturers to absorb that sum of money out of the current year for which this estimate is being voted, and there is not much use of carrying in the Estimates an amount beyond the sum which can be absorbed.

The explanation of the minister with regard to the reason of the decrease is quite satisfactory to me, but I would like some further information as to the activities of his trade commissioners. I would like to know who they are, where they are located, what they are doing, and how hard they are working to assist the men who did answer the call in this country for production for national purposes of material for the manufacture of linen, and whether or not these producers are being treated by the trade commissioners with that consideration to which they are entitled. I am told that in England the warehouses are bulging to the roofs with linen, that ther never was in England the scarcity that is alleged, but that they had there all the yarn they wanted; and yet the manufacturers and farmers of this country were pleaded with by this Government to "go to'it," to do their best, and to produce, and produce, and produce. Now they find themselves up against the wall,

and I want to know from the minister just how hard his trade commissioners are working. I want to know where they are working, and what they are
4	p.m. doing to ameliorate this unfortunate condition into which the flax industry has been thrown, and I think probably unfairly thrown by-may I use a mild term?-English commercial greed.
I may be misinformed-if I am I would like the minister to tell me-but I wish to know whether it is true that during the war, and at all times since, the English linen producer, and the United Kingdom producer generally, has had all the yarn he wanted and that he could have supplied some to Canada and relieved the situation here, had he been actuated by a little more consideration of the difficulties under which this country laboured as the outcome of the war.
As to whether the trade commissioners are acting fairly by this interest, as by other interests-

I did not say "acting
fairly," my question was as to whether they are working actively.

As to whether they are working actively in comparison with their efforts in other directions I think I can answer that by a very strong affirmative. They have received special instructions outside of those relating to their general duty, and I must say with regard to our present staff of trade commissioners that I think they are a set of men whose intelligence, honesty, and assiduity cannot be successfully criticized. They work not only because they are paid a salary, but because they are instructed in their work. They are enthusiastic in the performance of their duties, and the intimate relations the department holds with them, and the statements of the men who travel in those countries where they are and should come into contact with these commissioners, affords evidence to back up the assertion that I have made. I honestly believe that we have amongst our trade staff to-day, our commissioners abroad, a better set of men than we have ever had. I believe that we have a most satisfactory staff which will compare with the staff maintained by any other country.
Now as to what it is possible for them to do, that is a different matter. If prices have gone down, the shoulders of all the trade commissioners are not strong enough to boost those prices agaisnt world conditions. That is a situation that the trade itself comes up against and that the com-

missioners are powerless to overcome. All they can do is to seek out any possible avenues that are available for the exchange of these products in the countries in which they have their work set out, and that they are doing. But the countries are not very many that take these products. Great Britain itself has absorbed them in the past. The manufacturers there have paid highly for the flax seed, and the fibre as well, that they have got in Canada, and they prize these commodities just as highly as before. But they have stocks on hand more than sufficient for their own use, and they will not buy fresh stocks when they stand face to face with the market, in a measure, as our own producers of flax fibre stand. I am convinced that three or four years ago the conditions of the market were such that neither the United States nor Great Britain could, in justice to their own people, satisfy the requirements of our people. They did it to a certain extent, but gradually we came up against the impossibility of getting any supplies from either one country or the other- There is one thing that lights up the situation somewhat, and that is that this factory which is at present making fibres from these yarns has demonstrated that Canadian material and machinery, backed by Canadian enterprise and technical skill, can make the product from the root up in this country of such a quality as will bear comparison with the product turned out in Ireland, Belgium and other countries where this industry has been established for many generations.

I am very much pleased to hear that the minister has such a remarkably active and well equipped staff, and I am sorry indeed to find that he is forced to confess that his staff is absolutely helpless under the circumstances to afford any grain of comfort at all. But in his long narration concerning his excellent staff the minister has not told us of a single instance where any of his men have endeavoured to ameliorate the serious conditions under which our producers of flax are labouring. His men, I presume, are scattered all over the world. What I asked him was whether he has been getting reports from any of his staff containing suggestions that would assist our people here to dispose of the product of their factories that they cannot work up for the foreign market because the banks have refused them accommodation. The situation is more serious, I think, than the minister realizes. To use his own words, the manufacturers of this country undertook to establish equipment for the working up of these products, but only one manufacturer lived up to the undertaking. I would like to know the names of the manufacturers who failed to redeem their promise. Let us see who they are and why they failed.

My hon. friend pushes me pretty tightly up against the wall. What answer would he make if he were in my place? I will put myself in his place and answer. He does not impugn the efficiency of our trade commissioners. If he did I would have to defend them, and I could do so with a perfectly honest heart. But what can men do under the circumstances? My trade commissioners cannot go down into Ontario and lift one ounce from the load these people have to bear. The only hope of relief is in extended markets. To secure extended markets you must go outside of Canada. That is what our trade commissioners are doing, but they are up against the conditions of the market in other countries just as our people are up against the conditions of the market here; and if the market is overstocked, and consequently prices are low, no trade commissioner can raise those prices or alter the general conditions. My hon- friend spoke about those manufacturers who gave a certain undertaking. Our action was in the nature of trying to get people to supply the need that existed at the time; and when the War Commission took the matter up they had communication with more than one manufacturer, but only one succeeded in establishing the proper equipment, and he is to-day manufacturing the goods. The others did not come under any bond and they could not be compelled to do anything. They would only get the subsidy when they produced the goods, and they would take upon themselves the responsibility of the equipment in view of the bounty which would be paid for the three years after the war while their equipment would be working. I do not think I can give my hon. friend any clearer answer than that.

In looking over the trade papers I notice that a short time ago there was a convention in Brussels or Antwerp of representatives of various countries with a view to fixing the prices of linen fibre and linen, the trade being in a bad way in all countries. Did we have a representative there?

I do not
remember if we had one at that particular meeting, but I should not have much faith

in the power of a convention to fix prices which would stand against world conditions as they are to-day.

It was a meeting of flax growers and flax manufacturers at which England, Ireland, Germany, France and Japan were represented, and they made an effort to fix a minimum price of, I think, seven cents. I do not know whether they were successful or not. But the condition is world-wide, it is not confined to Canada alone.
Certainly not.

I would not think of criticising the members of this commission, but I understand that the purpose of the commission is to give information to the general public. Now it may be working very hard, but if it had done its duty, it seems to me it should have got information two or three years ago as to what would be the actual conditions after the war, because, if this had been done, many of our farmers in Ontario would not be in their present unsatisfactory position. We were led to believe that there was a great shortage of flax and linen and that for some years to come the price would be on a paying basis. But after going into the business quite extensively our farmers find this year that all along there was plenty of yarn and linen piled up in the Old Country. Why did not the commission know those conditions and report them to our farmers? I noticed in one of the leading papers a few days ago that some one had stated that Ontario fibre was not as good as Belgian or Irish fibre. We have at Ottawa a flax expert who states that the best quality Ontario fibre is equal to any that is produced either in Belgium or Ireland. The other statement will certainly hurt the sale of our fibre. Why does not the commission criticise that adverse statement? Why does it not come out and tell the world that our fibre is as good as any fibre that can be produced, as we are led to believe it is? Japan and many other countries have warehouses right in Belfast, where, from the information I have received, they manufacture more linen than in any other part of the world, and people can go to those warehouses and select what they want. The buyers on the other side do not want to buy it in lots of a few pounds, and they will not come over here and buy it in Ontario because the manufacturers there buy different grades of fibre. We should have a warehouse there as other countries have to which our fibre could be shipped and 
where the purchaser could select what he wanted and pay for it. I think that this commission should surely be able to furnish some information to the growers of Ontario. Commissions of that kind should give full information about conditions in other countries. I feel quite satisfied that if the farmers in Ontario, and I think some in Quebec, had known one or two years ago what the conditions would be they would not be suffering the losses that they are likely to suffer this year.
The farmers of Quebec did not go into any large cultivation of flax.
Some small quantities were produced there, I believe.

May I ask the minister whether the manufacturers of these linen goods in Canada are giving to the trade commissioners that co-operation which is necessary if trade in the foreign fields is to be captured? I understand that the trade commissioners are a thoroughly capable body of men who are performing their work in an excellent manner. But it has been stated and we had a man speaking on this subject a short time ago in one of the rooms in this building-that the manufacturers of Canada have not any agents in the foreign field. I know of two men who have been all around the world, who visited every commercial field, but wjho met no salesmen anywhere representing Canadian firms. It seems to me that the Canadian manufacturers of linen are relying entirely upon the Government and upon the trade commisioners to advance their interests, and I do not think it is possible for the trade commissioners to do anything of that kind. The trade commissioner cannot have that intimate knowledge of every line of business which is necessary to the effecting of a sale. Salesmanship to-day involves an accurate knowledge of the article which it is intended to sell, and it is impossible for the human mind-in this case, for the trade commissioner-to grasp the salient features of every line of business, and thus be able to effect the largest possible number of sales. Has the minister any information which would show whether or not Canadian manufacturers are actively engaged in the promotion of Canadian business abroad? If they are not, it is time they awakened to the necessities of the situation.

Are we under any moral or legal obligations to pay this

$2,000 to the producers of flax yarn? Are we free to withhold the bounty?

The answer is a very plain one, and as a business man my hon. friend will understand it. The Government entered into a contract; that contract has three years to run and is limited as to the amount that1 can be paid under it. These men, with that signed contract, put their money into the equipment of the business. They put in a splendid equipment and are doing excellent work. The Government, therefore, is not in a position to say: Well, we have not as much money as we used to have; we do not want to pay you anything; we will slide out. As to the question put by the member for Regina (Mr. Cowan), there is a negative and a positive answer. Some manufacturers are wide awake and have their representatives wherever in foreign fields there is a fair chance of making a sale. The trade commissioners were never instituted, never paid, never instructed, to make any sale for any particular party or for any particular corporation. They are not sales agents; the sales agents are to be put in the field by the men who have the commodities to sell. There never can be a thoroughly good foreign trade for this country unless the manufacturers cooperate with the trade commissioners and follow up the information furnished by them. To make your sale of goods to a man you have to sit down before him, first, a thorough master of your business in all its details so that you can meet his every argument, and then if modifications are suggested you have to be able to tell him on the instant: I will take you on that; you have made me an offer; I will take it. Where would your trade commissioners be if they were placed in a position of that kind?
Now, with reference to the flax industry, there are men engaged in that business who are fully alive to the situation and have their representatives in the Old Country and perhaps in other places. We are in constant communication with them and through our trade commissioners in England we help them all we can. I do not think they have any fault to find with the extent of the co-operation offered by the Trade and Commerce Department.

I thank the minister for the explanation which he gave us as to its being impossible for the Canadian people to break this engagement entered
into with the producers of flax yarn. But at the risk of being tiresome may I just observe how this affords a striking example of the unwisdom of endeavouring to bonus into precocious economic life one industry or another? When a Government by bonuses or protection undertakes to interfere with the law of supply and demand, in the long run they do more harm than good.
What harm has that factory done?

The member for Duf-ferin (Mr. Best) has just placed before us the fact that inducements were held out to the farmers of Canada to go largely into flax production. It was held out to them that there would be a market for flax through the manufacture of flax into yarn as a result of this bonus.
Oh no, the hon. gentleman is altogether wrong.

I had nothing to say about the manufacturers here. In fact, I believe that if we had three or four similar factories engaged in the manufacture of this commodity, there would be a sale for it. I was only criticising the work of the commissioners in not informing the farmers of the conditions on the other side.

My hon. friend may deduce from the facts different conclusions than those which I arrive at. But I think I am right in saying that he is my authority for the statement that the increase of flax production was substantial; that farmers in Ontario were led to believe that it was a wise thing to go in for the production of flax; that they devoted certain of their land to the production of flax rather than to the raising of other crops, and that today the market for flax is broken and they are suffering a loss. Now I think it is a fair argument that these farmers proceeded as they did because of the hope and the expectation that there would be a considerable market for their crop, and that hope and expectation was no doubt based, in part at least, upon the action of the Government in granting this bonus upon flax yarn. My right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) shakes his head. It seems to me that is a reasonable deduction to draw, and I think most members will draw that deduction. What has happened? The market for flax has slackened and there has been a loss. You will generally find that this is what happens when you bonus, when you stimu-

late artificially one industry rather than another, because you cannot control world supply and world demand, and market prices, in regard to the great staples of production, are created by world supply and world demand. Of course, we must not do what is ethically wrong, seeing that the manufacturers of yarn have altered their position by reason of this contract entered into by the Government. Yet, while perhaps in war conditions, it may not have been improper to give this stimulus, I have always the gravest doubt about the advisability of following such a course, either in war or in peace. I would make this observation, that we have here another example of the unwisdom of interfering with economic laws; that, as a rule, this interference does not help, but hinders and hurts the general interest. Let me give an example. Prior to 1846, protectionist sentiment in the Old Country, largely looked to agriculture; the Corn Laws formed the great keystone of the protectionist arch, and it was agreed that by maintaining what was practically prohibition of imports until the price rose very high on the introduction of foodstuffs into Great Britain, you maintained agriculture in a flourishing condition and that tended to keep people on the land and to maintain an agricultural position.
They are doing the same thing in England now.

And they will have the same disastrous results as they had before, I have no doubt. Let me make my point, my hon. friend will or will not agree with me as he sees fit. The point I want to make is that, during these years, while the agricultural interest in England was supposed to be helped by the introduction of heavy duties on foodstuffs coming into that country, the agricultural interest suffered very severely. Every [DOT] few years, parliamentary investigations had to be held to examine into the cause of agricultural distress. And why? Because in lean years, when the harvest was small, the prohibition or the impediments to allowing food to flow into Great Britain were such that prices became very high and rents were fixed on a very high basis. Then when there was a bountiful harvest, prices tended to drop; but rents tended to remain where they were, so that the only people who benefited in any way by the system were the landlords, and even they did not really benefit, because the misery which was thus
[Mr. McMaster.l
imposed on the bulk of the people reacted upon the landlords as well. The committea will pardon this digression, but I want to emphasize the point, and all my reading and experience go to confirm the notion which I have held for years, that it is a great mistake to interfere with economic laws, and that harm and not good is the inevitable consequence of the pursuance of that policy.

My hon. friend has made his point, or he thinks he has. My contention is that his point was not well taken, and I do not want his argument to proceed from a false assumption. The argument of my hon. friend was: You set up a factory to manufacture yarn and textiles from flax fibre-by setting that up, and in setting that up, the idea you had m mind was to stimulate the production of flax in this country-that idea got abroad amongst the farmers; they produced flax and produced it and produced it on that assumption-and now your factory takes but a small proportion, and the flax producers find themselves with large surpluses which they cannot market. That argument does not apply in this case. The point had in view by the War Trade Board and the Government was not of giving this bonus to a factory to stimulate the production of flax in this country. To a certain extent, the factory would call for a certain proportion of flax that it required for its manufacture. The object in view was a war object and no other. What is wisdom at one time may, as my hon friend said, be unwisdom at another, so that we have to go back to the time which produced the action. What were the grounds upon which the action was taken? I think it well that the committee should know these grounds :
Whereas it appears that no linen thread or yarn has come forward from Great Britain since the first of January, 1918, for the manufacture of Ashing nets, or shoe hemp for military and agricultural harness, or for the manufacture of aeroplane cloth,-
The demand for which was very insistent at that time.

linen thread for military boots,-
And military boots bad to be provided
-machine thread for the manufacture of agri cultural and military harness, or yarns and threads for civilian use in Canada.
That was the basis. It was the utter lack of those things necessary for those purposes that induced the War Trade Board, on the suggestion of the Govern-

ment, to see whether or not they could bring about the manufacture of those things to apply to that necessity and that emergency. That was the purpose, and my hon. friend was quite wrong in placing it upon the broader ground that we went into this bonus for the purpose of stimulating the production of flax in this country. The production of flax in this country, not stimulated much by this, although that provided a certain limited market, was stimulated by the high price that prevailed for both the seed and the fibre, and the impression that those high prices or profitable prices would prevail for a long time and that, therefore, the farmer would have a remunerative result from his labour if he put his labour to the production of flax seed and fibre. My hon. friend (Mr. Best) finds fault with my poor trade commissioners because they were not prophets.
Not with them.

My hon. friend is not a prophet; I am not a prophet, and to put a man back five or four years ago in the turmoil of world conditions and ask him to tell your farmer in Ontario just what conditions would be four or five years afterwards, is giving the man no show at all unless the Lord Almighty pointed out to him what he should say. Only inspiration could do that; no human knowledge could. Therefore, I think it is not right to ask from our trade commissioners what they cannot do. The Jap, my hon. friend said, went ahead and put up a great warehouse and stocked it with flax fibre and seed and went on the market to sell it. I am afraid my hon. friend has hold of a bit of a fairy tale in that regard. Anyway, if' that were a fact, the Government could not follow that course; it dould not take wheat or flax or any other product that is made and establish warehouses and put in stock, and then either wait until somebody came to buy or induce them to buy.
I refuse to be charged with opposing this grant to the flax industry of Canada.

I did not say
that.

I was referring to the hon.
member for Brome (Mr. McMaster).

I hardly think my
argument is open to that.

My complaint is that the
bounty is not half a million or a million dollars. We send our fibre from here to
the Old Country where it is manufactured, and then hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of the manufactured article is shipped back to Canada. Would it not pay the people of Canada better to give a bounty so as to have the manufacturing-process done in this country? I was not criticising the item at all. What I was criticising was this. I believe this commission could have found out what quantity there was on hand each year. Perhaps I may be wrong in that, but I think it could have been done, and if that information had been given to the farmers there might not have been quite so much flax produced, I did not say that the Japanese had a great big warehouse in Belfast. I said they had a warehouse there, where every variety of their fibres and seed samples could be shown. A small room, with one man to look after it, would do. A buyer could look over the fibre and seed and decide how many bales of fibre or how many bushels of seed he would take. The cost would be very small. If the farmers of Ontario are going to produce fibre, I think the Government should certainly establish a small warehouse there. I hope no hon. member will think I am criticising this bonus. If this bonus had not been granted, we would not be in the position we are in to-day as regards the fibre industry.
ME SUTHERLAND: I think we have wandered a little from the item before the committee, which is to provide $26,000 for a bounty on linen yarn spun in Canada from Canadian flax. Last year the item was $30,000. It is admitted that, there are immense stocks of flax fibres in the hands of the growers in this country. As a rule 1 do not favour bounties, but if ever there was a time when we were justified in passing such an item without criticism, it is now. I do not favour reducing the item to $26,000. I could not help but feel that if we had someone in this country whose foresight was as good as the backsight exhibited by the hon. member for Brome, we would have a world-beater. I did not approve of the bounty When it was first introduced, because I believed that flax growing was an industry that was peculiarly adapted to a country where cheap labour was plentiful. If you study the history of flax growing and linen production all over the world, you will find that it is most successful where cheap labour prevails, such as in Russia, India, Belgium, and Ireland. These countries have excelled in the growing of flax and the manufac-

ture of imen. During the war, however, there was such a tremendous demand for linen, and the price went up to such a figure, that many people went in for the growing of flax, for they knew that climatic conditions in this country were ideal for its production. Well, the price has fallen since. The deflation in the price of flax seed, linen and hemp is only what you find in the wool industry as well.
We had linen industries in this country before this item was placed in the Estimates. There was in the constituency that I represent a small factory engaged in the manufacture of linen. It is now a branch of the factory that is established at Guelph. They have been manufacturing Imen very successfully, and their success is in no smail measure due to the fact that this item was placed in the Estimates. Unquestionably there are immense quantities of flax in the hands of the growers for which they can find no sale to-day. I do not believe we are justified in encouraging its manufacture into linen in this country and therefore I am heartily in favour of this item in the Estimates. Instead of reducing it to $26,000, I think we would be quite justified in leaving it at $30,000.

I want to disagree as strongly as I can with the attitude of my hon. friend from Brome in this matter. To my way of thinking, he is a most unprogressive gentleman. If his policy had been followed, Canada would never had got to where it is to-day. I think he would make a good old-time Conservative. This item in the Estimates has been a benefit to Canada, even if the flax market is broken today. We have proved that we can raise in Canada the very .best kind of flax for fibre purposes, and- that is worth a whole lot more than the amount it has cost us in the way of bonus. This industry is not for to-day only; we shall have a flax industry in Canada for all time to come, employing thousands of men, and bringing profit to the farmers who raise the fibre. I think this is the proper course to follow if we are going to develop this industry in Canada. We must start it by just such means as we are adopting here. I think we ought all to support the item, which will encourage the development of this industry.

The minister asked us to excuse him for this bad legislation on the ground that it was adopted in war time. I think the minister really should be excused because any ministry that thought winter time was the time to grow flax in

this country must have been more or less confused. The Order in Council for the encouragement of the flax industry was passed in September. That fact alone, I think, shows that the minister must have been very much confused. Had he waited for a more reasonable time, he would have found that the war was over, and he would have avoided the criticism he has received this afternoon from his own supporters for his lack of knowledge of the conditions in the flax industry. An hon. member has asked whether it was not the whole Government that was responsible for this Order in Council. I suppose the whole Government would be responsible. Certainly Parliament was not responsible. Parliament was not consulted about the matter, and had nothing whatever to do with it. The Government acted on the principle of divine right, at the time they were doing things by Order in Council instead of submitting them to Parliament. They passed this Order in Council to grow flax in the winter time instead of waiting until the House was in session, which would have been time enough, if this legislation was really necessary. I say it was a bad move on the part of the Government, and the minister deserves the criticism he has received from his supporters this afternoon.
Flax grows better when it is sown on a snowbank.

The particulars concerning this item are not to be found in volume 3 of the Auditor General's Report. I would be very grateful if the minister would indicate where they are to be found. I owe the committee an explanation with reference to the previous item. The minister and I, I am quite sure without any bad faith on the part of either of us, misled the committee when we agreed to let the first item stand. I stated that the particulars were not in volume 3, but in volume 4, and the right hon. gentleman was under the same impression. Now I wish to correct both my statement and his impression. The particulars are to be found in volume 3, and if the minister desires to return to the item I withdraw my objection. Will he tell me, if he can, where the details of this flax item are to be found in the Auditor General's Report?

If I am to answer my hon. friend exactly according to his question, the details of this item will not be found until it has been worked out on the basis of production and the accounts

hare been paid and audited. That will appear in the Auditor General's Report, probably of 1922.
We mean last year's expenditure.

Last year's expenditure, if anything, was very slight, and I am not sure that there would be anything in the Auditor General's Report this year concerning it. In the report of next year, the audited accounts will be found. I am glad to go back to item ,346, but I am sorry to have to say that my faith in my hon. friend's general veracity has received a severe shock. He told me, with such an honest look in his countenance, that the details were to be found only in "Z" that I took his word for it. After this' I shall have to query when my hon. friend makes a positive statement.

Has the minister any encouragement to offer the flax growers of the country for the future? What my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) stated a few moments ago is absolutely true. There are many flax growers throughout Ontario who were encouraged to take up this business by the facts placed before them by representatives or supporters of the Government. They went ahead and have produced a crop which they have yet. They have been at great expense, having paid out money which they could have spent to better advantage in some other direction; and now they have flax on hand which they are unable to dispose of. I do not say this in any unkind spirit or for the purpose of criticising the Government for having given encouragement to this or any other-industry. I believe they are justified in taking such steps as they deem fit from time to time to encourage an industry which they hope will turn out profitable to the producers. But I would ask the minister if he has any advice as to the future to offer these men who have seriously gone into this industry, made large expenditures, purchased machinery, and put up buildings to take care of their crops. Would he advise them to continue or to withdraw from the industry, and take up some other line instead?	.

I certainly
would not advise them one way or the other, and it would be a pretty bold man, I think, who would take the responsibility of giving advice to people as to how they should employ their enterprise and spend their money on production in the future.
The best that could be said about it is that men must use their judgment in the light of their knowledge of the world and of business. You have to make your investment on the basis of your conviction as to what the future has in store, and a .man would assume a great responsibility if he presumed to give advice to people to go on producing flax because year after next they would obtain splendid prices. It is not possible for one to make such a prediction, and if it were, it certainly would not be possible under conditions as they exist at present. If my hon. friend thinks for a moment he will realize the truth of this. Still, we cannot stagnate. If a government is to do anything to help conditions, it must proceed on general lines, advising that we produce all we can and raise all we can; but, after all, the producer himself must be his own judge as to whether or not he will follow such advice, even though it be given with the very best intention and on the strength of information * available at the time. We all know that things change, and sometimes the change is so rapid that what appeared to be the height of wisdom at one time in the prosecution of an enterprise might be the height of unwisdom at another time, and a policy deemed advisable previously might later on turn out disastrously. I have no specific for that sort of thing, and if my hon. friend has any, I should like him to give me the formula.
How many factories have actually been established which are entitled to the bounty?
One.
Are they entitled to the bounty whether they produce yarn or not?
The bounty is paid only on the production of yarn.
On what basis is it given?

It is paid on the basis of so many cents per pound, based on the "lea"-their measurement-which signifies the degree of fineness or coarseness, as the case may be. The bounty is so many cents per pound of a certain fineness.
Would they receive any bounty merely as a remuneration for having put up a factory, or must they actually produce?
Nothing is paid except on what is produced.
What part of the $30,000 was expended last year?
What is the name of the company the minister mentions?
Just a moment.

The bounty
was paid from April 1, 1920, to December 31, 1920, on 110,0111 pounds of linen thread, the amount paid being $3,939.00.
What is the name of the company and where is it located?
The name of the company is Dominion Linens, Ltd., of Guelph.	[DOT]
What is the reason for the decrease this year?

I explained
that the bounty is paid on actual production. At present there is one factory producing, and it is without the bounds of possibility that that factory will produce enough during the current year to warrant the payment of $30,000, and it was therefore reduced to $26,000. I do not think it is very probable that they will absorb the whole of that sum, but if it is not earned, it wil not be paid.

The member for South Oxford, in his reference to this item, in speaking of the conditions in regard to the production of flax and manufacture of linen yarns, stated that one of the reasons why Canada was not able to compete with other countries was the cheapness of labour abroad. I think that another reason is the difference in climatic conditions. Climatic conditions in the north of Ireland particularly, in Belgium, Holland and Russia, are much more favourable to the production of a finer fibre than can ever be produced in Canada under the climatic conditions that prevail here. The conditions here will prevent the Canadian producer from ever competing in the markets of the world for finer fibres. There is another reason which apparently has not been considered this afternoon in discussing this subject. That is the fact, that while in the Old Country they produce flax for the fibre only, in Canada I understand they try to produce flax at the same time for both fibre and seed. Now it is impossible to produce the finer grades of fibre and save the seed at the same time. If you produce the fibre to the stage where the seed ripens you have coarser fibre as a result,

and consequently it will not be possible for the Canadian producer to compete in markets of the world in the producing of the finer grades of this commodity.
I have no desire to prolong the debate on this item, but in view of certain definite statements which have been made by the last speaker I feel it incumbent to at least say a few words.
I have not completed my remarks. Does the hon. gentleman wish to ask a question?
No. Let the hon. gentleman proceed with his speech.

If my hon.
friend will allow me, does he not think it would be more appropriate to discuss the matter of trade commissioners on the item relating to them which comes up a little later?

On general principles
I have no doubt the minister's view is correct, but I merely wish to refer to the matter in passing in order to emphasize a point which was alluded to by the hon. member for Dufferin. Now you have trade commissioners at Yokohama, Havana, Bar-badoes, Rio de Janeiro, Vladivostok, Shanghai, Cape Town, Buenos Aires, Rotterdam, and other places whose title terminates in the same manner as the last one I quoted.

That is an
awful mean way of swearing.

Although there are trade commissioners at all these places there is not a single one in the city of Belfast.
Now I ask the minister why it is that the Government, although it obtained last year $30,000 for the encouragement of the flax industry and is now asking for a sum of $26,000, has not any representative in the city of Belfast to look after the interests of the Canadians who have this yarn to sell?

In the first
place the capacity of the Dominion is limited.- There are a great many other cities in the world besides Belfast where we have no trade commissioner. As my hon. friend said we have about thirty commissioners, but even those are not sufficient to meet the needs; we have to send them where we think the best general advantages can be derived. At the present time I would imagine it to be a little bit dangerous to be in Belfast.
I think a trade commissioner would be just as safe in the city of Belfast as he would be in the Bahamas, Shanghai, or Vladivostok.

But you hace
to keep indoors there.

It seems ridiculous for
the Canadian Government to be endeavouring to promote the production of flax in Canada and to be granting bonuses for this purpose, that it has not followed the matter up by appointing a resident agent in the city of Belfast, the world centre of this particular branch of trade, to look after the interests of Canadian producers.

I wish to say, in reference to the observations of the hon. member who has just spoken, that he takes upon himself a very serious responsibility in criticising the support that the Government is trying to give to the establishment in Canada of an industry that has such immense possibilities. I am sorry that world conditions so far have prevented manufacturers from Ireland, and I may say even manufacturers from Belgium, who are experts in the cultivation and manufacture of flax, establishing mills here and taking advantage of this bounty to encourage the spinning industry in Canada. It must be patent to any one that it is the height of folly for us to continue to be the hewers of wood and the drawers of water for the countries of Europe-for us to produce our raw material and send it over there to be manufactured and re-sold to us in the finished state.
There seems to be a desire not only in the House but in the press to discount the ability of Canadian growers to produce flax

of high quality. A prominent Belgian who was in this country a short time ago, in the course of an interview given to a representative of the Montreal Star, stated that Canada grew as fine a quality of fibre flax as could be produced in the civilized world; but that Canadians so far had not been able to handle their flax as scientifically as growers in Belgium, Ireland and other countries. Why, Sir, the very object of establishing a department of fibre in connection with the Experimental Farm was not to show farmers how to grow flax-[DOT] that is easy enough-but how to handle it after it is grown. You may produce a crop of flax the acre value of which might not represent twenty-five dollars after it is harvested, and yet that very same flax handled under expert direction and properly retted and scutched might represent a value of from $300 to $350 an acre. It is for that very purpose that we want expert direction through our Department of Agriculture. Then, having produced a quality of flax equal to the best that can be produced in Europe, the Department of Trade and Commerce, through this bounty, can encourage the spinning of the fibre into yarns. This means spinning it into threads from which the linen is woven. As a result of that encouragement a mill was established in Guelph by Dominion Spinners, Limited, the purpose of which was to use Canadian flax fibre for the making of yarns, and then in their adjoining mill to weave the yarns into linen. The quality of their goods is attested by the fact that the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the King Edward Hotel and other leading institutions which demand a high quality of linen for their tables are buying their supplies from Dominion Spinners, Limited; in other words, they are buying linen which has been woven in a Canadian mill from yarn spun from Canadian-grown fibre. The Brooklyn Linen Mills of Belfast, Ireland, have already been looking into the possibilities of growing fibre in this country with a view to the establishment of linen mills here. I hold, Sir, in view of the fact that we have such a tremendous potential water power in this country, and that we can grow fibre here of such excellent quality, there is no earthly reason why with proper encouragement we should not have the flax spinning and weaving industries developed here to their highest possibilities. I submit that if several spinning mills were established here-as I hope they will be- 
the $25,000 or $26,000 appropriated for bounties on the production of these yarns would be too small, and it is my cherished hope that the industry may so develop and such a large amount of yarn will be spun as to require even a large appropriation for this bounty.
This afternoon, while this discussion was proceeding, I was engaged in my room dictating a long letter of protest to the Montreal Star in answer to an article which appeared there a week ago to-night. A Mr. Ireland, of Ireland Bros., large linen manufacturers of Belfast, allowed himself to be interviewed by an ignorant reporter of the Montreal Star-ignorant on this subject; I will qualify it to that extent; absolutely ignorant of the subject about which he was seeking information. Mr. Ireland, in expressing his optimism and hope for the future of the industry, made the statement, that with the present condition of the industry throughout the world there is a total visible supply of not one-third enough fibre to operate the mills in Ireland alone for a single year. Yet notwithstanding that condition, and the impossibility of the Baltic and other flax-growing districts getting back to normal conditions within a reasonable time, the price of this commodity has been depressed to a point where it is now below the cost of production in this country. That is a very unfortunate circumstance, but it is not one to discourage us, because production costs last year were abnormal by reason of the very high rate of wages. Mr. Ireland expressed the opinion that these conditions impelled the conclusion that in the very near future there must be a large increase in the consumption of fibre, and that as soon as the retailer commenced buying linens there would be a demand on the manufacturers for their goods, and having eased themselves of their stocks, a demand would spring up very quickly from the manufacturers for the limited supply of fibre that was now available. Therefore there is every possibility that our growers will come through with a very fair profit if they will have patience. But the point in this article that I object to, and the point which I drew to the- attention of the chief of the fibre department of the Experimental Farm, is this. The interviewer asked Mr. Ireland what did people in Ireland and the rest of Europe think of Canadian flax. He said: Oh, Canadian flax does not meet with very much success. He could not say anything against

its quality, for it was good, but the flax in this country was grown mostly for linseed. Now, that was an absurd statement for him to make. It is true that in the West flax is grown for linseed, but in Ontario and Quebec we grow flax for fibre exclusively, and we have developed a quality equal to the best fibre grown in any part of the world.
I urge, Sir, that it is the duty of the Government at this critical time not to get discouraged. Our growers are not discouraged. They will grow more flax next year, but not so much as in former years; they are going to feel their way. I have expressed the opinion in this House time and again that the duty of our growers is to develop quality rather than quantity, that a hundred acres of good flax from which good fibre can be produced is better than five hundred acres of mediocre flax, the fibre from which you cannot find a market for, against the competition of Russia, Japan and other flax-growing countries. I hope the Government will stand to its guns and will follow up its good work by establishing a demonstration plant in the district where fibre is mostly grown, and will by research work encourage the adoption of better methods and better mechanical appliances. There is no reason why we should not have by this means, a flax industry developed to the limits of its possibilities, and an industry which will add enormous potential wealth to this country.

I cannot allow the statement of the hon. member for ' South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) to go unchallenged. In my constituency there are five flax mills which took care of a production area last year of over two thousand acres. Some of these mills have been in operation for fifty years or more and their business has been conducted in such a way that their fibre has been sent to Belfast and is considered of the very best quality in every particular. There is no question about the capability of the people of my county to raise the very best quality of flax fibre. I merely make that statement for the purpose of correcting the hon. member for South Renfrew.

I am pleased indeed to hear the correction made by the member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong). I am pleased also to see the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) here. During the progress of the discussion I looked around for him, and as my hon. friend has
made a specialty of this subject and has discussed it on numerous occasions on the floor of the House, to take the matter up without Ms being present seemed to me to be like trying to play Hamlet without the star performer, the Prince of Denmark. I was glad to hear from him the facts of the situation in regard to the production of fibre and to know that in Ontario at least they have not been trying to grow flax both for seed and for the production of fibre. That was attempted in the early stages of the production of flax, but without satisfactory results. I am sure that the information which has been given in regard to this matter by the member for East Middlesex will be of much interest to the general public.

A certain amount of confusion constantly arises from the fact that .we can grow flax for seed as well as flax for fibre. The characteristics and the methods of cultivation in the growing of flax for fibre and the growing of flax for seed are entirely different. In producing flax for seed in the West they sow one-half bushel to the acre and as a result they grow a short, stocky straw which throws out its branches and has many seed bolls on it. The statistics show that in good soil and under favourable conditions they have reaped a crop of as high as twenty-eight bushels to the acre. Their purpose is to grow seed; the fibre is of no consideration whatever; for generations back the straw has been burned as waste, there being no use for it. In Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, and the provinces where we grow for fibre, the seed is of an entirely different character. It is seed which has been cultivated down through successive generations, having been grown originally in Riga, Russia, developed in Holland and then sent out here and grown as it is in Ireland-Dutch Child seed, we call it. This seed, instead of being sown one-half bushel to the acre, is sown a bushel and one-half to the acre, and the result is that instead of growing a short, stocky straw, they grow a long, lean straw running from thirty-six to forty-five inches high, the whole outer surface of which is covered with this fibre. The seed that is grown for oil contains twenty-five per cent more oil than the seed which is grown for fibre, therefore when you have to sell the fibre seed to the oil mill a deduction of value is made because oil cannot be produced from that seed in as great quantity as it can be produced from the regular oil seed. It is owing to the confusion with regard to our growing th it



flax in the West and growing this other type in other parts of the country that tne countries of Europe are getting mixed up as to our capacity for the production of flax. It is necessary, therefore, by propaganda and advertising to keep before the public the fact that there are two distinct varieties, one having no connection witn the other, one produced for one purpose md one for another. The statement that flax cannot be grown for fibre as well as for seed is also erroneous to some extent, because this is the only country under God's sun where we can do both. We pull the fibre flax up by the roots at a time when the seed in the boll has not been fully developed-is not ripe. But the seed is left in the straw and it goes on to maturity while the plants are in the stock, and there is no very great deterioration in its quality. The Government demands, of course, that all seeds exported to Europe for growing fibre must be certified as to quality, must show a purity of not more than one weed seed to the ounce avoirdupois, which means one weed seed in 3,390 seeds, and that they must germinate ninety per cent. My hon. friend will admit that if we grow from our fibre straw a seed that will germinate ninety per cent-and it does germinate, as has been shown by test, up to ninety-five and ninety-eight per cent

it can scarcely be said that we cannot grow fibre and, from the crop grown, obtain seed as well. We do obtain the seed, but it is not our purpose to sell it to the oil mills if we can find a market for the product in the form of fibre; because last year it had a value of $10 a bushel for fibre whereas its value for oil seed is not half that amount at the present time. There does not appear to be a market for the seed for fibre, because of the large surplus of Holland seed. The flax growers who grow for fibre have to sell their seed at twenty per cent under the price obtained for the oil seed of the West because their fibre seed does not produce the same amount of oil.

The hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) has just substantiated the point I made, to the effect that when you try to produce flax fibre and seed at the same time, the quality of the fibre is depreciated. You cannot produce the high est quality of flax fibre and produce a ripened seed at the same time. During the course of the discussion this afternoon the minister said that he did not desire to give advice to the farmers or to anyone else in a matter of this kind. But after the discussion which has taken place here to-day

I think he should arrive at the conclusion that is is not advice the farmers want, but information as to the proper methods of handling this product. If the Department of Trade and Commerce will supply the correct information to the men who handle this product, those men will have received from the department all they should expect, and all, I am sure, that they desire.

It has been stated during the discussion that this is an old in-i dustry, having been carried on in Canada for fifty or sixty years, and that we are>
producing here the very best quality of fibre in the world. That being the case, I do not understand why the minister has been giving a bounty for the encouragement of the industry. Bounties are usually given to encourage new industries, and before a bounty is granted the minister has to be satisfied that the industry in question is of a national character and that it has a future. What is the reason, then, for the granting of a bounty to this industry?

The
statement I made is with regard to the production of flax seed and flax fibre. I have in my riding no industry like this that would require a bounty. There is in Canada only one industry for the manufacture of fibre and that is located at Guelph.

We have the raw material in abundance and of the veiy best quality, so that in the state to which we have developed it, we have for the last fifty or sixty years been capable of controlling the markets of the world. Why then, having such splendid material, should we not go on and develop and manufacture it further without any bounty at all? If we have to get a bounty for the manufacture of flax which is of the very excellent quality which the hon. member says it is, would not the same argument apply to every industry in the country? If a fisherman says that he is going to produce boneless codfish or that he is going to manufacture canned halibut or anything like that, where he takes a stage in advance in the production and output of fish, then he can come to the Government and say: "If you give me a bounty on every can or barrel of fish, I will produce a more advanced article." In that case, I think the department would say: "You have the article; you have your opportunities in the world, and you must hold your own or go under, just as the case may be, because we cannot follow a general policy of granting bounties to every industry in this country." I understood the minister to say that there was in Canada only one mill that

was spinning this kind of yarn, and the bounty goes only to the spun material. Therefore, if all of this $26,000 is to go to one mill, I would like to have a little further explanation from the minister. Until I looked a little more closely to this item, I thought the bounty went to the farmer; that when he produced the flax in some stage or another, he was getting the bounty. The farmer, however, does not get the bounty at all. All this afternoon we were making a lot of noise about what the farmer was going to get, when the farmer was not entitled to anything, because this item says that the flax must be spun. If there is, as I understand the matter, only one factory in Canada in which this process is carried on, I do not quite like the idea that we are going to give this $26,000 to one concern. I should like a further explanation why we had so much talk about the farmer over-producing and this bounty being given to relieve the farmer when he does not get it at all.

Ask the hon.
member for Brome (Mr. McMaster).

I am discussing this question with the minister now, and I give it as my opinion and practice that I always stand by and get information from the department which is the responsible source. I would not even take chances on going to South Oxford, although, perhaps, it is the most prolific source of information known to the human race at present. If the farmer does not get this money, and if there is only one man who does the spinning, why should we give him, or let. him earn, $26,000 out of the depleted treasury of this country? The minister told us a little while ago that the bounty on oil goes to the farmer who has a side-show of oil producing. If the farmer who produces flax must be encouraged, why does he not get the bounty, without waiting until somebody takes the flax and spins it and then the latter gets the bounty for doing so? The spinner does not take any chances at all; he need not buy from the farmer, and he will spin and manufacture only as he sees an opportunity of selling. I cannot quite understand why he is getting the ' bounty and nothing being given to the farmer, who may have a large stock of this material piled up. On the other hand, the moment the manufacturer sees an opportunity of selling some of this manufactured stuff, after he has spun the fibre, he gets a bounty. I do not see the consistency of that course.

I think my
hon. friend could not have been here when I explained why this bounty was granted in the first place.
