If he had, he would have known that it was a war measure and that it was not given specifically in order that more flax might be raised, but it was given specifically in order that linen thread, of which there was an absolute lack in this country, might be furnished to the fishermen and boatmen and harnessmakers and all those that required it as an absolute ingredient in their manufactures. My hon. friend might use the same argument with reference to an industry in which he is interested. Why was a bounty given on steel plates or iron? Why was the bonus not given to the men who dug the ore out of the mine? That is susceptible of an answer much the same as this. What the country and the department wanted at that time was not flax seed or fibre; it was what was never made in this country before, something of which there was an absolute lack and which was necessary for all those different purposes that I mentioned. We wanted to find a man who would spin the flax fibre and make it into thread, which would be used in those various works of necessity and out of which ultimately the textiles would be woven. My hon. friend proceeds on the wrong ground when he proceeds on the idea that this was a bounty to stimulate the production of flax seed or fibre. Indirectly, it had the effect of stimulating the production of flax. The bounty is open to any mill that will put in the machinery and manufacture the article. If my hon. friend or any friends of his would put in the amount of money necessary, erect the machinery and spin this flax from the fibre, they would have a share of this bounty; it would not be given to one. But this is the only mill which has equipped itself and is, consequently, the only spinner of flax thread in the Dominion. -

The minister has
drawn an analogy between the granting of a bounty to the spinner of flax fibre and the granting of a bounty to the producer of steel. When he talks about a bounty to the producer of steel and pig iron, we are dealing with a concrete case and we know exactly the circumstances. There was no distinction of ownership in that case; the same man who made the pig iron owned the raw material.
Not necessarily.

There was only the
one specific case in Canada, or two at the outside.

My hon. friend is wrong. The bounty was given on pig iron with which was mixed a certain and quite a large proportion of foreign iron ore. It does not necessarily follow that the man who made the pig iron owned the iron mines.

There was never anything else. There were only two companies in Canada that ever got much advantage [DOT]-The Dominion Coal Company, and the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, and they both owned their iron ore. The bounty was never given to anybody simply because he had ore and was not manufacturing it. I do not wish to detain the minister with his Estimates for one moment. I only wish to tell him that we are seem to be following a different practice than has been usual when considering Estimates. A minister used to get through his Estimates without very much trouble from his own side of the House, but it is different to-day, and I would suggest to the minister that he should caucus his Estimates so that when he brings them down here he will only have to battle with those who are not in his confidence. Practically the whole afternoon has been taken up with sniping from behind the minister. He has had very little trouble indeed from this side of the House.

Was this Order in
Council passed under the War Measures' Act?
Yes.

The minister has just
admitted that the Order in Council was passed under the War Measures' Act. I gathered from a previous statement he made that we had made a contract for three years, and that we could not, if we were to keep our faith as a nation, rescind the contract until the end of that time. I am not sure that I am quoting him correctly. Well, in answer to a question from the hon. member from North Cape Breton and Victoria the minister has just made the statement that so far only one mill in Canada has availed itself of the advantages of this contract. I suppose the minister is providing in his Estimates this year for the subsidy which that mill will earn?

Or any other
that may qualify for it.

My hon.
friend's statement is not right in this respect. If this mill with its equipment can make a sufficient quantity of linen thread to make it necessary for us to pay out $20,000 as a bounty upon the number of pounds that it makes, it would get the $20,000, and my hon. friend would be right in his reasoning, but at its present rate of production it would not get that amount. If another mill equipped itself and produced thread it would also share proportionately in the bounty, which cannot exceed $25,000.
I thought it was $26,000.

The contract
is $25,000, and if ten mills were producing, and producing at an equal rate, each mill would get only one-tenth of $25,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The vote is for $26,000.

That includes
the expenses of supervision.

I allowed $5,000 for that,
leaving a bonus of $21,000. The fact remains that the minister is providing for a preferred dividend of 7 per cent on an investment of over $300,000 for three years. Now, either the minister has in mind that this particular company will get the whole subsidy, or that some other company will avail itself of a part of it; otherwise, it would not be necessary to vote this full amount. I think it would be well for the minister to take the committee completely into his confidence in view of the opposition that has developed from his own supporters. The opposition to this item, I gather, is largely upon the ground that this particular mill subsidized by Canada, with its dividends guaranteed, is not taking care of the crops which the farmers of that district have been encouraged to grow in anticipation that they would be able to sell them to this mill. The mill will not take the flax, and consequently the farmers are the losers because they could have utilized the land for growing cereals or for dairying or some other purpose.

We have heard a good deal to-day about developing the flax industry in this country, but if my knowledge of the trade is at all correct, Russia grows two-thirds of the flax production of the world, and exports one-half of its product to Great Britain, Germany, Prance and Belgium. I am not sure that it is a wise policy to subsidize an industry that comes into competition with the cheap labour of Russia. We might invest our money in something that would be more suitable to this country, and that would give us a better return on the investment.
There is another feature. On the one hand, hon. gentlemen who represent constituencies where fibre is produced for this mill complain that it is not buying the fibre. I should like to know how this mill is dealing with the people of Canada in selling its manufactured product. Is their selling price up to the very limit they can obtain under the tariff laws of this country, or is there any advantage to the Canadian people in purchasing linen from this particular company?

My hon.
friend, I think, was scarcely fair in trying to make it appear that a very large amount of opposition had developed to this particular vote on this side of the House.

That is how it looked to
us over here.

But the glasses probably were arranged so that it might look that way. Neither was my hon. friend quite fair, I think, in stating that all the incentives to the raising of flax in Ontario and other parts of the Dominion were centered entirely on the fact that here was one mill that was manufacturing a small proportion of linen thread. That was not what caused the development and expansion of the flax fibre and seed industry. As I stated before, and as my hon. friend will readily admit, it was the general conditions of supply and demand throughout the world which made the price for flax fibre and flax seed very high and remunerative, and it was that high price which stimulated the growth of flax fibre and seed. The market has suddenly receded, as it has in a thousand other instances, and consequently there are stocks on hand that cannot realize the old price. There may be stocks on hand which cannot realize a remunerative price. This is but a small item in the incentive towards increased development in the production of flax. My hon. friend wants to know how
they are selling, and so on. Well, as I mentioned a while ago to the committee, only about 110,000 pounds has been manufactured up to the end of 1920, and that would go a very small way in the manufacture of textiles. I imagine they are selling at as good a price as they can obtain.
Is the number of pounds mentioned by the minister the full capacity of the mill?

That was only what was spun by the mill in a limited time; it does not take in the whole year, neither was it the full acapacity. Your capacity increases according as you bring in your units. What the full capacity is I do not know.

I hope the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) does not propound the doctrine that because Russia in the past has produced two-thirds of the total flax fibre production in the world, and, owing to cheap labour, was able to produce it at a low cost, therefore we must lie down or get out of the way and let that country continue this production. We produce a quality of fibre in this country that is superior to the great bulk of the fibre produced in Russia. Hon. gentlemen do not seem to understand the conditions that were responsible for this bounty. Primarily, I suppose, it was due to war conditions, because we had mills that could weave linen cloths for aeroplanes, but we could not get the yarns. We had raw fibre and were sending it across the seas to help the Mother Country, but we could not get a pound of yarn here, and the only mill we had was shut down because it could not obtain supplies of yarn to carry on manufacturing. Cotton looms were installed and, I believe, cotton was spun. Now, the production of fibre by the farmers a,nd the small co-operative mills of this country had been possible only by exporting the material. During the war it was felt that if we could spin the fibre here and produce aeroplane cloths, we should be doing the Empire a great service. But, there was the fact that we were allowing our fibre to go out of this country to be spun into yarns in Ireland, Belgium, France, and elsewhere, where there are spinning mills. My hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), said he understood that we have been manufacturing these yarns in this country for a period of sixty years. He is entirely wrong in that impression. Except through

the hand loom in the home of the habitant, we have never before spun yarns in this country. This bounty was given to encourage the establishment of an industry which would enable us to use our materials right through the various stages of production to the finished article, linen. No one would imagine that a mill would begin operations on the assurance of a bounty for one year. The mills asked for a bounty of $25,000. That was the maximum that could be given in one year, and it was to be given for three years. It was divided into three classes, a bounty of three cents, six cents, and nine cents per pound, according to the quality of the yarns spun. The three cents per pound bounty was given on all yarns between ten lea and twenty lea, which is the coarser quality. The yarns of a finer fibre, between twenty and forty lea, were granted six cents a pound, and all above forty lea were given nine cents. The object of the higher bounty was to encourage the spinning of a finer and better quality of yarns in this country. That, of course, is a matter of great importance to the grower as well as to the spinner, because if we are to spin yarns of sixty lea and upwards, it is necessary for the farmers to produce the higher quality of flax.
Were these various qualities of yarn spun in the same mill?
Yes. Now, the spinning of yarn of good quality is not a question that depends on any method of handling in the mill; it is a matter of having a quality of fibre that will produce fine yarn.

Were these various
very fine qualities required for war purposes?	.

I am informed that yarn that would spin sixty lea was of ample fineness for the purposes of manufacturing aeroplane cloth, which was the matter * l principal importance at that time. It has been stated by a prominent linen manufacturer that ninety per cent of the production of all linens in the world are manufactured from yarns that are spun under one hundred lea of fineness, We have already produced yarns in this country that have spun up to one hundred lea, which is an exceptionally fine quality. We need not worry ourselves if we are unable to produce a quality fine enough to compete with the finer yarns spun from Belgium flax retted in the Courtrai district. If we can produce a quality sufficiently high to be included in the ninety per cent of the
	_
total world production, we are producing an article which, I think, should command sufficient sympathy from this House to ensure its development. My hon. friend from Cape Breton said he thought we were helping the farmers. Well, so we are. If we can develop the spinning of a finer degree of yarn by developing our own spinning facilities, naturally it follow's that the onus is on the grower to produce a finer fibre that will give us the better quality of yarn. An acre of flax will produce three hundred pounds of fibre, and that fibre may be worth anywhere from fifteen cents per pound to seventy-five cents per pound, according to quality. Whatever be the quality of the fibre, it has taken the same amount of labour and the same area of land. But it is a matter of great importance to the producer whether he gets fifteen cents a pound or seventy-five cents for the product. It is a total difference of $1,200 per ton in price, or as will be seen, $180 an acre. I think that we should urge our people to produce, not so much with a view to quantity a~s for the purpose of securing as good a quality as can possibly be had, because it is in the hope that we may produce an article of the highest quality that we shall ultimately displace Russian flax from the American, and even from the Irish, markets. Russia will not bother us in the production of flax for a few years to come, and unless she improves her methods she will not be a serious competitor in the higher grades. But if our ambition stops at the coarser grades, then Russia will be a serious competitor against us in the years ahead. In order to encourage this industry a bounty of $25,000 a year was granted by Order in Council as a maximum to be continued for a period of three years.
Now people might naturally say, in fact the statement was made at the time, "There may be half a dozen mills start up, and in that case we will not get this bounty on our production. We will only get the bounty in the ratio that our production bears to the entire production; and it may be that if five or six mills were producing enough to absorb $100,000 on the basis of the bounty given, that each mill would only get twenty-five per cent of that bounty to which it might be entitled if there was not competition." Nevertheless we hoped the assistance given would attract the Irish mills to this country, and that we would ultimately develop a large and extensive spinning industry in this country, because


it follows as surely as that the night follows the day that to develop the spinning industry means the development of the growing industry, and that is where the advantage to the farmer comes in. I submit that in fairness to the manufacturer who started the mill in question, it , is our duty to keep faith with him. I hope that if we keep faith with him we will find before the expiration of the term for which this bounty is granted, other large firms in Ireland desirous of establishing mills in this country.
Would there be an ample market for the yarn spun in Canada?

There is a market in the world for more than Canada could possibly produce if she had twenty mills. The spinning capacity of the world to-day is not sufficient to supply the world's needs for linen at the present time.

My hon. friend said something about the mills wanting a! guarantee of $25,000 before they would enter, into this undertaking. Does he mean that they wanted such a guarantee from the Government of Canada, or from the city of Guelph?

I do not think I made myself clear to my hon. friend; I certainly did not mean to create such an impression. What I said was that they were presuming at the time that half a dozen mills, maybe a dozen, might take advantage of the encouragement as proposed for the establishment of spinning mills in this country. Now the maximum amount of the bounty was $25,000. If twelve mills of equal capacity started operations and each mill earned according to the rate granted, a bounty of $25,000, it would instead of getting the full bounty, receive only a ratio as one of twelve.

If my hon. friend is right in saying that there is an ample market at the present time for yarns spun in Canada, and that even if several other mills were established they could not produce all the yarns that the world's market could absorb, I fail to see the necessity of a subsidy to bonus such an industry. The idea of such a subsidy is to protect an industry during its earlier years against competition; but if my hon. friend's statement is correct, and I take it that he is an authority on the subject, I fail to see why this industry requires assistance. It should not need aid if there is an ample demand
for its product in the markets of the world. I would like to have some explanation from my hon. friend as to his reasons for supporting the granting of a subsidy when, according to his own statement
6 p.m. of a moment ago, no subsidy is necessary for the establishment of the industry.

My hon. friend propounds a question in regard to a matter which seems to me very clear. The bonus would be applicable in this case just the same as it is in the case of the iron and steel industries, or any other industry which it is desired to encourage.

My hon. friend will permit
me to point out that the iron and steel industries in Canada had to fight their way, in the matter of marketing their products, in the face of very strong competition. The point as to which I would like my hon. friend to give some enlightenment is that in this case, according to his own statement, there is no competition- there is a demand for the entire production not only of the existing mills but of other mills that might be established. The hon. member also said that we need not fear competition from Russia, which used to produce most of the flax consumed, for years to come. The case of the steel bounties is not at all parallel to the present case:	In the one there is competition, and
in the other there is not at present, according to my hon. friend, a sufficient supply to meet the world's demand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there any possibility-, by sitting a few minutes longer, of putting this item through before the committee takes recess?

I think there is every
possibility of putting the item through if the Minister of Trade and Commerce would promise to control his followers.

If my hon. friend will
pardon me. I do not wish to unduly prolong the debate, but a point has arisen upon which I would like some enlightenment before I am ready to support this vote. The point is the one I have endeavoured to explain. We are asked to vote a subsidy for the encouragement of this industry and the hon. member (Mr. Glass) has just informed the committee that there was such a demand for yarn that even if several spinning mills were established it could not be supplied. If that is true, it seems to me no reason exists why we should assist this industry

by voting it a subsidy. The reason for the granting of a subsidy is to protect an industry against competitors in the markets of the world. In the case of the present industry not only is there no competition but there is an insufficient supply of the material-that is accepting the statement of my hon. friend. Under the circumstances the matter wilil stand further investigation, and I therefore respectfully beg to differ from the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) who said that the question could be disposed of in a very few minutes.
At Six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at Eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering the Estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Item 346 had been allowed to stand. We had considered item 347, which has not yet been adopted. Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, when the
committee rose the question was on the advisability of continuing the bounty to the flax industry in view of the fact that there is not a sufficient supply of fibre to satisfy the excessive demand. Therefore I do not see why a subsidy is necessary to encourage the development of the industry. The principle underlying a subsidy is that of protection to the particular industry during its infant years so that it may survive undue competition of stronger rivals. I would be very much interested to hear the hon. member (Mr. Glass) who is known as an expert on this subject, give the committee his reasons for supporting the grant of such a subsidy.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman draws the deduction from my statement that because there is an unlimited demand for the visible supply of fibre there is no reason why encouragement should be given to the manufacture of the raw material in this country. In theory his deduction may seem to him to have some force. It was pointed out this afternoon that although this industry had been in existence in this country for a period of fifty or sixty years-and I may tell my hon. friend that he would not have gone astray if he had said "that it had been in existence for a period of over two hundred and fifty years-yet we had not made that substantial progress in it that might reasonably

have been expected. The total visible supply of flax fibre to-day is not sufficient to keep the British spinning mills alone em>
ployed for one year. But that visible supply will also be sought by the spinning mills in Belgium, Austria, France, Germany and other parts of the world. Therefore it is a fairly reasonable statement to make that the present supply is not at all sufficient to meet the demands of the world. Now, my hon. friend asks the question: If there is an unlimited demand for flax fibre, why is there any need of protection? I answer him by saying that there is a demand, but there is a suspension of that demand for the time being by reason of what is generally conceded to be a consumers' "strike." The impression prevailed that all commodities had reached such a high cost that there must inevitably come a reaction, and the consumers of linen came to the same conclusion and they quit buying. The result was that the wholesaler ceased buying his supplies from the mills, that reacted on the mills and they had to suspend operations, and at present they are operating on very short time and are loaded up with their manufactured product. If my hon. friend's question applies to the immediate present, I would say that the demand having been temporarily suspended, and the supply in the mills being ample under those circumstances, there is a supply for which there is no call at present.
Since when?

Practically since last September. It has been intermittently stagnant from that time on. The consumers' "strike" still continues and therefore the manufactured goods are not moving. But so soon as the usual channels of trade become active again the demands of consumers will react on the wholesalers, and they in turn will be eager to relieve the manufacturers of their present stocks.

Although this temporary
condition of slackness of demand has existed only since last September, I would point out to my hon. friend that the subsidy was introduced under the provisions of the War Measures' Act in 1919, if I remember rightly.

The conditions arising
out of the war only added force to the arguments in favour of a subsidy to encourage the development of the flax industry in this country.

Was there not at that time such a tremendous demand that although

all our mills worked day and night they could not satisfy the war-time requirements ?

No, my hon. friend is
entirely wrong. There was not such a demand as the mills could not satisfy, but there was such a dearth of raw material that they could not produce the yarns with which to manufacture cloth.

Did I not understand the
hon. gentleman to say that there was such a demand for fibre in England that our Canadian weaving mills could not get their supply, and that the demand for their products was out of all proportion to their means of supplying it?

I am sorry I cannot make
myself clear to my hon. friend. I do say that there was a demand for the cloths, the resultant product of the weaving mills, which could not be supplied at that time because the available supply of flax fibre, which is the raw material of the spinning mills, could not be produced, and the only weaving mill in Canada at that time was the Dominion Linens, Limited, in Guelph, they having established a mill there at a cost of $750,000. They had previously been importing their yarns, the manufactured article from the fibre, and from those yarns weaving their cloths. Due to the war conditions then prevailing and the necessity for aeroplane cloths, Great Britain, Germany and all the belligerent countries forbade the exportation of the fibre and yarns and of any other flax products. What was the condition in Canada? We had a mill but that mill was stagnant because we could not manufacture our fibre into yarn to keep the spinning mills going.
Because you could not get the yarn from European mills?
Precisely.

Then there was such a demand for the yarns that the Canadian weaving mills could not get their supply to keep them going. Therefore my argument is that if there was such a demand for yarns, there is no need of protection to the spinning mills.

My hon. friend draws a
very unreasonable conclusion. Does he think for one minute that by reason of the demand for fishing nets, aeroplane cloths, harness threads, shoe threads and the other products of flax fibre it was reasonable under the pressure existing at that time to start their manufacture here, although the war might be
over in six months or a year, when the large manufacturers in England, with their experience and their organization spread over centuries, with all the facilities and advantages which were at their command, might be in a position to crush any small mill which was started in Ontario? Surely it is unreasonable for my hon. friend to take that position.
Not at all. I will ask for further information from my expert friend. Under normal conditions before the war, was there an excess of supply in yarns, or was there an excess in demand?

Before the war there was an adequate supply of yarns and an adequate supply of fibre,/ eighty per cent of which was produced by Russia. When the war started the York Street Spinning Mills of Belfast saw the possibility of great diminution of the supply in Russia, so they sent an expert out to look over the field in Canada and see whether they could produce here the raw material for their linen mills. The man whom they sent out was a Mr. Lockhart, who is still chief of their organization. He came to the little village of Park Hill in the county of Middlesex and from that centre he established mill after mill in adjoining districts, and as a result of the success of their effort the acreage was increased year after year until it had run up to between three and four thousand acres. This Belfast mill had not known that they could use any flax fibre produced in Canada. Not a dollar's worth of flax fibre had ever been exported from Canada to European countries. Our sole market had been in the United States, in the thread mills of Massachusetts and New Jersey, and the result was that our growers were compelled to take the price fixed by the mills in Andover, Massachusetts and the other mills in New Jersey. They could scarcely get a price that would yield a profit sufficient to encourage any expansion of the industry. Now, Russia got out of the market completely and the demand continued to increase throughout all the years of the war, chiefly through the demand for aeroplane cloths. As a matter of fact, the manufacture of flax into linen for table-cloths and things of that kind was prohibited in Great Britain and Germany; the governments took control of the whole supply of linen and directed its manufacture to the production of aeroplane cloths. The hon. gentleman suggested this afternoon that

Russia was able to grow eighty per cent, or four-fifths of the world's supply of fibre, and he asked what was the use of Canada producing fibre in the face of that fact. Well, would he suggest that because Russia, Argentina or other countries ean produce wheat at a lower cost than we can, our farmers should discontinue the growing of wheat? I hope that this country will build up a great home market in which they can use all their wheat and all the fibre and linen that we produce. The point I want to make is that we have grown fibre in this country for two hundred and fifty years, but we are very little advanced in our methods of production-and so it is throughout the world-over the methods that were employed six thousand years ago. Canada has done something in the development of mechanical appliances for handling these crops, but in my opinion she has not measured up to her responsibility in the matter of research work with a view to improving the methods of retting this fibre. We have manufactured throughout all these years, but we have never been able to establish an industry here by which we could spin our yarns.
Why?
Because the production of fibre was small on account of the expensive methods of handling, on account of the cost of labour as against the low cost of labour in Russia.
Could we not import the fibre as Ireland did?
Yes, we could import the fibre, but we could not get labour with which to operate our spinning-mills at four times the price they pay in Ireland.
I speak of the conditions prior to the war.

I, too, am speaking of conditions prior to the war. We have open markets in the world for raw fibre just as Ireland has. But my hon. friend knows or should know that the conditions of labour prevailing in Ireland were such as to involve a standard of living that would not be desirable for the workingmen of this country, and I hope that the standard of living of the workingman in this country will never come down to the point which it reached in Ireland. Before the establishment of this spinning mill we did not know the quality of the fibre we had been able to grow. We accepted the price for 
our fibre fixed by the spinning mills in the United States. The lower grades of tow- the waste or by-product of the manufacture-were suitable for a good deal of the material which they manufactured, and not having any market for our fibre in our own country we exported our superior material at a price based on that of the cheaper tows which are produced to-day. When we established the spinning mill-
When was that?

A year ago. When we established the spinning mill we commenced to show by actual demonstration what we could do in this direction. Hon. gentlemen may theorize all they like about Canada not being able to grow flax, but when we delivered the goods, when we produced an article from our own raw material, we demonstrated that we could grow a fibre that would spin yarns up to sixty lea. There has been some difficulty in getting the machinery necessary to the development of the business up to the standard we aim at. This mill which has been in operation for a year has been able to get a certain amount of machinery with which to carry on the development of the coarser grades of fibre, but machinery for the spinning of the finer yarns is under order and when it is installed we shall be producing a quality of fibre away above that which we are producing now. If for no other purpose than to encourage the production of a higher and better quality of fibre I submit that the encouragement which has been given to the spinning industry has been fully justified. Hon. gentlemen have expressed the view that if the bounty re-acts beneficially upon the farmer, they are enabled to view it from a more favourable standpoint. That may be all right so far as it goes, but my argument is that the development of the spinning industry has shown the farmers and the growers what they did not know before: that they are able to produce a fibre that can compete with the best standards of fibre in Europe; that they do not have to take twelve and one-half cents a pound for it; that in the future, instead of receiving $250 a ton, they may reasonably expect a permanent market at a price of from $750 to $1,000 a ton.

I do not think the hon. gentleman has answered my question at all. He has repeated the theories that we heard from him this afternoon and that we had heard with great interest at various times prior to that. The question I put to him is this: If there was a demand under normal conditions, setting aside abnormal con-

ditions created by the war, and if the supply was sufficient for the demand for spun yarn, then there is no field for such an industry in Canada, and it would be better if we diverted our energies and capital to more profitable propositions. If, on the other hand, there is not a sufficient supply, then the demand is incentive enough to our manufacturers to start such an industry, and thereby the necessity for such a subsidy disappears- That is the point I tried to make clear to the committee this afternoon. I wanted to be enlightened but I am sorry that I have received very little enlightenment on the subject so far. There are only two alternatives-whether the demand exceeds the supply or the supply exceeds the demand. If the demand exceeds the supply, there is no necessity for a subsidy to protect such an industry. If the supply exceeds the demand, there is no field for such activity, and the Government .would have been better advised to encourage industries with greater prospects of success.

As my hon.
friend (Mr. Vien) has, after this arduous series of debating conflicts with my hon. friend on this side, come to the conclusion that he has not received any enlightenment and does not see any prospects of receiving any, probably it would be better for us now to leave the general question with which this is incidentally connected and go back to the appropriation itself.
Is the minister not of opinion that the principle at stake, underlying the appropriation, is of some importance?

If my hon.
friend will allow me to present, for a moment or two out of his precious time, my point of view, I shall be very glad, and then he can go on again. This appropriation is for a special purpose. I explained it early in the afternoon. During war time and at a period when it was impossible to get any linen thread in this country from outside sources, and when there was a great demand for these linen yarns for war and for peace purposes here, under the War Measures Act the Government, on the recommendation of the War Commission, proposed, for the purpose of getting these yarns spun in Canada and getting a material which we could get in no other way, that we would give a bounty if anyone be found to put in the equipment necessary for spinning yarns, none of which equipment we had had in Canada before. We had not spun an ounce of linen yarn in Canada previously to that. As a result
of inquiries and after a good deal of negotiation, we proposed a plan of giving for three years a subsidy, of the limited amount of $25,000 a year, not to exceed in the three years $75,000, and to give that on a poundage basis to men who would put in the equipment and spin the yarn, such subsidy not to be paid during the continuance of the war, but to commence after the determination of peace and to be continued for three years thereafter. The reason for that was that, during the war period, owing to the scarcity, the price would be sufficiently high to be an inducement to remunerate them somewhat at least for the extra equipment put in, but their hard time would come after peace had been declared and after prices had taken the fall which they inevitably would take. Under the War Measures Act the Government made a contract with those people. We have paid them upon the first year of their contract; we are to pay them on two years more of their contract, and I am simply asking for this appropriation to enable us to do what our part of the contract asks to be done in an obligation out of which no reasonable person would, I believe, think we ought to attempt to crawl for any reason whatever. We are not discussing any broad principle of subsidies to flax interests or to the making of yarn. This is a war child, born of war necessity, a contract entered into by the Government under the War Measures Act, and we ask the committee to give us this appropriation to carry out our part of the contract.
Does the minister consider that this will be a permanent industry in Canada or that there is an opening for such an industry?

If we take the vote on the ground on which I have stated it, it would make no difference what I thought in that regard. This is a contract we propose to fulfil. We ask the committee to give us this appropriation in order to fulfil the contract. My hon. friend is a business man; he knows what contracts are, and I do not think in his heart he has any objection to the Government fulfilling a contract into which it has solemnly entered. All these extraneous things in the discussion are very important, but we are not discussing to-day a permanent policy of subsidizing either the spinning or the production.

But there is this much to
be said:	The Government is now before
the committee and subject to the judg-

ment of the committee as to the wisdom of the policy adopted at that time and as to the wisdom of the conract entered into by the Government with that company. The minister has explained to the committee that this was a war measure adopted for war purposes. Other industries were started during the war for no less important objects. For instance, new industries had to he started for the manufacture of shells, cartridges and a number of other articles of great necessity during the war. The prices given for such articles were the incentive, and the Government never thought of resorting to a subsidy or bonus to those industries no matter what amount of machinery they had to purchase or what amount of experience they had to acquire. The Government simply placed contracts with those firms to deliver certain quantities of materials, and they never introduced the idea of protection by way of a bonus to these industries for war purposes. In the present instance the Government has adopted a different course. Owing to the necessity of getting the yarn, not only did the Government offer the inducement of the general conditions prevailing, but they went a step further and offered a subsidy amounting to $25,000 a year if a manufacturer could produce sufficient to earn this subsidy. This was a departure from the general policy which prevailed at that time. The minister, to explain his position, brushes aside the principle at stake and says: "Surely the committee will not refuse the Government the fulfilment of their contract. The Government have entered into a contract and this committee cannot put that contract aside." I am in favour of the flax industry in Canada and of developing the establishment of mills to spin yarns from fibre produced in Canada, but before we decide to protect such a new industry I put to myself and to my right hon. friend the question: Is there a field of operation before it which holds out prospects of success in the future? My right hon. friend evades that question. He brushes it aside altogether, and says it is not the question involved, that the only question involved 'is the fulfilment of a contract. In my humble opinion, the Government were wrong in making a contract with such a company, because the demand for this material at that time, as the minister himself has admitted, was just as great as for the material turned out by any other industry started during the war period. So I say from the point of view of [Mr. Yien.1
the contract the Government was wrong in entering into it. Before we determine to protect a new industry by way of this subsidy to be paid during three consecutive years, I put to myself and to my right hon. friend the question:	Is it an industry
which has any chance of success in the future? I have failed to draw either from my right hon. friend or from the previous speaker any answer to that question, and to my mind that is the whole principle which underlies this vote; it is not the question of the contract, but the question whether we should protect such an industry. If there is a chance of this industry surviving we might consider this vote, but we have not been enlightened on that point so far.
What amount was paid to this corporation last year? I notice the vote this year is $4,000 less than last year.

Is that for the calendar
year? I understood the right hon. gentleman to say it was up to December 31.
Yes, from the time production commenced.
Were any further amounts paid after December 31, last.
No.

So the figure given by my
right hon. friend covers the fiscal year as well?

Accounts may
have come in which have not yet been paid, but they will be accounts for work done during the remaining months of the fiscal year.

Would my right hon. friend tell us why the Auditor General's report is absolutely silent as to the expenditure during last year? As it is an expenditure during the period covered by the Auditor General's report, it seems to me the matter should have been reported on by the Auditor General.

The Auditor
General's report that my hon. friend has before him deals with the fiscal year ending March 31st, 1920. This production was after the expiration of that fiscal year.

I understood the minister to say that $3,939.77 was paid in bonus to this industry last year. How much

was paid for supervision, or for nursing this war baby?

The large
amount of $197.

That was all that was
paid out of the appropriation of last year?

Up to that
time.

Item agreed to.
Bounties on Crude Petroleum, administration of the Act, $3,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This item has already been considered to a certain extent. The hon. member who objected to its passing this afternoon is now willing that it be re-considered.

I find, at page Z-23, Volume III, of the Auditor General's report, that the monies expended in the period covered by the report were paid, not to individual farmers, as was intimated by my right hon. friend this afternoon, but that all the monies have been paid to companies, some of which have received very large amounts. I would like the minister to tell exactly what these companies are, and where they are operating.

I am afraid
I cannot give my hon. friend the information with reference to all these companies or individuals who have been recipients of the bounty. The law states to whom the bounty shall be paid. Our supervisor makes certain that the oil which has been raised has been correctly represented, and thereafter the bounty is paid at the rate of one-and-a-half cents, I think it is, per gallon. As to the composition of these companies or the associations of the farmers amongst themselves I have no know, ledge at all, and no information which I can give to my hon. friend.	_

I think the minister
might supply the committee with more information than apparently he is willing to give. This afternoon I raised the question whether this Government was paying this bounty to the large oil companies, such as the Imperial Oil Company, which is a subsidiary of the Standard Oil Company. I notice by the auditor General's report that the moneys which have been paid by the Government have been paid to corporations, not to individuals. If the right hon. gentleman will look at the list on page Z-23, volume III, of the Auditor General's report he will see that these corporations are apparently important concerns. I am
under the impression-I may be wrong- that they are subsidiary companies of the Imperial Oil Company. If they are, I think the principle is altogether wrong that this Government should give bounties or premiums to such corporations. Oil in this country is sold at very high prices, and I do not see why the Government should add to the already exorbitant profits made by these corporations by paying them bounties from the public treasury.

I am not so much
interested-
Perhaps the hon. member would permit the minister to answer my question first.

What I am about to say has to do with the point raised by the hon. member, and after I have finished the minister will be able to answer both questions at the same time. The point I want to raise is this: It would appear that under the law a bonus is paid for the production of oil. I do (not know whether it is payable only to concerns operating in certain provinces, or whether it applies throughout Canada. But I do know that the Government proposes to exact a royality on oil produced, and I should like to know how it is that we grant a bonus on the pi'oduc-tion of oil and at the same time impose a royality on that oil. That is what I cannot understand.

I think I explained this afternoon the origin of the bounty on oil. In 1904 the Government of that day removed the duty from crude oil imported into Canada. The production of oil in this country was at that time almost exclusively confined to some districts in the province of Ontario. Oil was produced in small quantities by a large number of people from individual wells, and some companies also produced on a small scale; and the bounty given at that time was a compensation to these people by reason of the introduction of free crude oil from the United States. That legislation was amended on two or three occasions so as to provide that the individual producers of oil, whether farmers or companies, should have the bounty paid directly to themselves. There are farmers who have oil and produce it simply in the line of their individual operations. They get their bounty on the amount they produce. There are associations of farmers in a small way that work a number of wells amongst themselves, and there are also companies, small and

large. The subsidy is paid to producers, whoever they are, whether individual farmers, associations of farmers, or companies. As to the quality of the oil, I suppose it was fixed at a standard corresponding to that of the oil allowed in free of duty. The law provided a specific gravity test of .8235. Those hon. members who are familiar with this subject will understand this matter better than I do; I do not know much about it myself. This provision first appeared in the Act of 1908, and has been in it since. This specific gravity test, I have no doubt, was applied to ensure that the oil on which the bounty was paid should about equal in quality the oil obtained from the United States and the condition is therefore precedent to the payment of the bounty, that it must he oil of a specific gravity of .8235. No oil gets the bounty if it does not fulfil that test. Very little of the oil that is produced in the West conforms to that test, and therefore hut a small portion of the bounty is paid on western production. Some is paid on oil raised in the vicinity of Edmonton. From the shales in the province of New Brunswick some oil is produced and that has to fulfil the test. The bounty is granted to all oils, wherever produced, that fulfil the requirements. The other question of my hon. friend, as to why oils on which a bounty is paid are made to contribute to the revenue, is explained in this way. Usually oil concerns that are started give promise of large results, and it is considered right that some royalty at least should be paid to the Government to pay for all the preliminary work which is necessary and for proper regulation and supervision.
May I suggest to the minister that the' wells of knowledge do not flow far enough in this direction? We are not able to follow him; we cannot hear.

I thought they were filled to overflowing. However, I will turn round and face my hon. friends. Now, to reply to my hon. friend on the other side who is thirsting for information, I find that there are companies and individuals mentioned in the memorandunr before me, and broadly speaking, I think there are more individuals or associations of individuals, than, companies, to whom the payment is made. Various names of companies are given, and my hon. friend has a suspicion that possibly they are subsidiaries of

the Imperial Oil Company. I do not know. No doubt they sell their oil after they get it. They would not raise it unless they had some prospects of disposing of it. The Imperial Oil Company may be the buyer of their oils; there may be affiliations between them-I do not know-but under the law I do not think I have any particular duty to enquire. It is the producer that receives the bounty under the law, and all that I have to do is to see that the party that produces the oil gets the bounty.

The question I am putting to the minister is this: Does the Government consider it fair that public money should be given to companies such as these under the law as it exists to-day? The question is all the more timely because if these corporations are rich, and are simply representatives of the very large oil trust called the Imperial Oil Company, the financial condition of Canada is such that we certainly cannot be extravagant and over generous in our treatment of them. I do not believe that any of these companies need any bounties if they are affiliated with, or related to, the Imperial Oil Company. If the law forces the Government to give these grants, I think the sooner that law is changed the better it will be for the country. I wish to draw the minister's attention to another fact. Looking over the Estimates concerning his department I have not seen any item covering the amounts which are to be distributed as bounties during the coming year?

These grants, as I have told my hon. friend, are the result of a law passed by the Dominion Parliament in 1904 and which has ever since been upon the statute book. By virtue of that statement preceding Governments have paid these bounties in exactly the same way as we are paying them now. If my hon. friend looks into the Estimates he will see that there are statutory payments made which appear in the Auditor General's Report. There are also payments made by virtue of votes passed by Parliament and debitable to the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

I understand that, but it does not affect my argument. I contend that whether an amount is authorized by statute, or whether it is simply voted in the ordinary way by the House of Corn-cons, it should appear in the Estimates to be voted for the current year. Such is the

case I contend, and to illustrate my contention I will mention the salaries which are voted every year for the judges, which salaries are fixed by statute. The amount for this purpose is what we may call a statutory amount, but nevertheless the Minister of Justice comes to the House every year, with the Estimates for his department and in those Estimates there appears a fixed amount from which will be taken the moneys to pay the salaries of the judges throughout the country. I contend that whether the money to be paid as a bonus to petroleum companies in Canada is a statutory payment or not it should appear in the Estimates. I would therefore like the minister to tell me where the money for this purpose does appear, so that we will know exactly what amount is to be expended in the coming year.

It is impossible for my hon. friend to tell, or for any one to tell him, the exact amount that will be expended during the year. That amount will be based on the number of gallons of this specific kind of oil which is raised and approved for bounty. The production may be large or it may be small, it varies from year to year, and you could put no sum in the Estimates which would represent the exact amount which may be spent. The contention of my hon. friend that in certain cases statutory payments appear in the Estimates is perfectly clear. I am not so certain that an amount, following the general rule, might not be placed in the Estimates to cover this item, but it would have to be an indeterminate amount. There would have to be a sufficient amount voted to cover the possible expenditure while the real expenditure,
9 p.m. owing to reduced consumption, might be very much less. But, as a matter of fact, the basic principle of the law is adhered to. The law states what shall be paid per gallon in the form of bounty. The administration of the law carries out the direction of the statute, and cannot go beyond that. So that whether the amount is put as an indeterminate item in the Estimates, no more or no less can be expended than what the statute calls for.

My point is that no minister of the Crown has a right to spend five cents of public money without having previously obtained from Parliament the consent of the representatives of the people to the expenditure of that money. If the minister will look through his Estimates, and I refer him particularly to page 24 where the Estimates of the Department of
Agriculture are set out, he will see where statutory payments are mentioned. The rule in this matter is well known. Does my right hon. friend seriously contend, in view of his very long experience in Parliament, that he has the right as a minister of the Crown, or that his department has the right, to spend money during the coming year without the representatives of the people having previously voted that mo'>ey? T do no+ think he will contend any such thing because it would be absolutely opposed to all rules of constitutional procedure. My right hon. friend is in exactly the same position as every one of his colleagues, and he cannot, after this session of Parliament is concluded, spend five cents, or a dollar, or ten dollars, without having previously obtained our consent as representatives of the people. The right hon. gentleman says "I cannot say to-night exactly how much money will be spent." Very true. But we do not ask the right hon. gentleman to state the exact amount which will be expended. We do want the right hon. gentleman to follow the rule of parliamentary procedure which requires that an amount for this purpose should be placed in the Estimates. That amount may not be all spent but it cannot be exceeded. The minister, through his officials and especially through this official whose salary we are now being asked to vote, should find out how much money he needs -he should fix the maximum which cannot be exceeded but which possibly will not be reached. This is the rule, and it must be followed by my right hon. friend as well as by every other member of the Government. If the right hon. gentleman refers to the Estimates, and the Supplementary Estimates, and the further Supplementary Estimates, of last year he will find nowhere an item covering moneys which have been paid for this purpose, even though the expenditure appears in the Auditor General's report. Under what authority did the minister spend that money? Under what authority did he spend money of which the Estimates of last year make absolutely no mention, and as to which they are just as blank as the Estimates of this year? How could he make such an expenditure without it having been voted by Parliament? I think, Mr. Chairman, that having regard to constitutional procedure the situation is very serious, and before we vote the salary of an official who is supposed to look after the administration of this law and distribute bounties to companies, we have a right to know how much money that official is going to distribute. Further-

more we have the right to find .out by
virtue of what authority the right hon. gentleman distributed money last year of which the Estimates contained no mention. I maintain that my contention is right, and that the Government has absolutely no power to spend any money unless that money has been regularly voted by Parliament.

My hon. friend has worked himself up to a wonderful pitch as a constitutional authority, but he has ended with one sentence which is the only thing that I shall advert to. It was that no minister has a right to spend a single dollar which has not been voted by this chamber. Let there we no doubt in our understanding of my hon. friend's statement. Now I will ask my hon. friend how much this House voted to the Minister of Justice? Will he be good enough to turn to the Estimates and see? Will he then turn to the expenditure and tell me and this committee whether he still considers himself to be right in his dictum? Or will he impeach the Minister of Justice for spending some millions of dollars in his department over and above what has been voted by this chamber?

Will the right hon.
gentleman allow me-?

Will the hon.
gentleman allow me for a moment longer?
The right hon. gentleman is putting a question to me.

I am, and I
will give my hon. friend an opportunity to answer it afterwards, and I would like him to bestow a little thought on it before he makes his answer. I am giving him an opportunity to be correct. Will he look at page 8 of the Estimates, item 4, and find out how much was voted by this chamber to the Minister of Justice for salaries and contingencies? It amounted this year to $190,832.50 with contingencies $25,000. Does my hon. friend suppose that all the expenses of the administration of justice will be paid for out of those two amounts? But that is all that was voted. And in his search after knowledge will my hon. friend turn to page 12 of the Estimates? There he will find that besides the amounts voted by this chamber $1,345,300 will be spent on the administration of justice under authority of statute, and under that authority alone. The figures there given are simply details, and not one dollar of it has been voted by this chamber. So that my hon. friend is not quite right in the stand which he has taken.

The right hon. gentleman was kind enough in his answer to adopt a tone which I am not going to copy, and he was also kind enough to ask me to bestow some thought before I replied to him. I always do think before I speak, and the answer to what the right hon. gentleman asks is very simple. I think that if he was a lawyer he would not have spoken in the way he has, because from a legal viewpoint his answer is no answer at all, and the question he put to me is no question at all. What I said is very simple, and I want the right hon. gentleman to understand and to bear in mind that when I am speaking I am thinking, and not to make the mistake of believing for one moment that I bestow no thought on what I am saying. We are asked to-day to vote the salary of an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which salary, if I mistake not, is fixed at three or four thousand dollars.

Two thousand
dollars.

This official has the duty of supervising the administration of a special law. This law sees to it that certain bounties are distributed to petroleum companies throughout Canada; and those bounties are distributed in accordance with that special law. My contention is very simple. I say that the amount which the Department of Trade and Commerce wishes to distribute for the coming year ought to appear in the Estimates in the same way as the salaries paid to our judges, so we may know exactly what moneys are being spent. The right hon. gentleman asks: Will I move for the impeachment of the Minister of Justice, because in the summary appearing in the index of the Estimates he has shown two amounts, one of $190,000 and another of $25,000 which do not cover the whole expenditure of his department? Certainly not; and the right hon. gentleman could not have been serious when he suggested such action. The amounts which are to be spent in accordance with the law and which are voted by Parliament can be expended by the department, but I say that those amounts have to appear in the Estimates so that every year the law as regards that expenditure will be again ratified by Parliament.
How ratified?

May I point out to my right hon. friend that there is a wide difference between a law passed by Parliament ten or fifteen years ago, providing for

the expenditure of a certain amount of money, and the expenditure by the Government of those moneys every year. It is a well known rule, and a rule which exists in England as well as here, that Parliament does not vote money for more than twelve months. That has been well established in England, and is considered to be one of the greatest safeguards of English liberty and freedom. My right hon. friend is not going to deny that. Therefore, as public moneys are not to be voted by Parliament for more than twelve months, another rule has been established in England-a rule so well known that my right hon. friend with all his experience will not deny its force- that Parliament has to meet at least once every twelve months. What does that mean? It means that every year the Government, through their ministers, have to come before the representatives of the people to obtain new subsidies, and the subsidies which are then voted to them are annual subsidies. The principle is the same, no matter whether it is a case of voting salaries to judges, or bounties to petroleum companies as in this instance. My right hon. friend will not deny that. So, coming back to my first argument when the right hon. gentleman answered me, I say that he ought to put in the Estimates an approximate amount of what is to be spent, which we are entitled to know. Does the right hon. gentleman contend for one moment that this committee is giving him a blank cheque for any amount at all? We are just as much entitled to know what the Minister of Trade and Commerce intends to spend as we were to know what the Minister of Agriculture intended to spend in accordance with laws passed by Parliament. On page 4 of the Estimates, the summary, I find the following: " Trade and Commerce, authorized by statute "- nothing; not a cent. So I think I have answered the question of the right hon. gentleman. I wish to be very respectful to him on account of his age and experience, but I am quite sure that his answer will be as thoughtful as the one I have given him.
I have stated my position, and my hon. friend in his reply has fled the coop.
What does that mean in English?

In English
that means that he has carefully avoided reaffirming the assertion which he made twice-it is on Hansard and he cannot get
rid of it-that no minister has the right to expend one dollar which has not been voted by this Parliament. Now, I am within the hearing of both sides; I am within the hearing of my hon. friend directly opposite, and he will not deny that.
It is quite correct.
I maintain the position which I took.
I do not think my hon friend restated his position, and I do not think he can maintain it.
Well, I tried to state it.

All through the Estimates there are certain sums which are voted and certain sums which are authorized by statue. For instance, in the case of the Department of Justice the sum of $1,300,000 for judges' salaries, authorized by statute, is absolutely fixed.
And has to be voted.

And has not
to be voted by this House. These sums that are authorized by statute are placed in the Estimates for information, but the House does not vote them. The total amount voted for agriculture this year was $4,502,139, but agriculture will spend this year an additional $1,100,000 which is authorized by statute but not voted by the House. In the case of pensions, $620,910 will be expended by virtue of the statute but is not and will not be voted by the House. So all the way through the Estimates. I am not prepared to say that as a matter of information it might not be shown under this vote that there is authorized by statute the payment by the minister of one and one-half cents per gallon for all crude oil of a certain test whic'h has been raised and certified to; it would be information, but you would not have to vote it. If my hon. friend's contention is that it would be useful to the House to have it appear in the Estimates that there was an expenditure authorized by statute, when I would concur with him, but I cannot agree that no single amount whether authorized by statute or not, can be expended by the mniister unless it has actually been voted by the House.

This being an oil item,
I would like to be able to pour some oil on the troubled waters. There is something to be said on both sides of the question. When the member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) says that no minister has the right to spend one dollar of public money until it has been



voted by the House he is absolutely right, and if my right hon. friend disputes that assertion he is absolutely wrong. But it does not follow that you have to vote it every year in the Estimates. The sums that are put in the Estimates as authorized by statute are there for information. The only point of difference between my right hon. friend and the member for Dorchester is whether it is necessary to vote these amounts every year, and on that point I am bound to say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is correct; these sums are voted by statute and the statute is a standing authority to the ministers concerned for the expenditure of the money. Where the amount is fixed, as in the case of judges' salaries, you have no difficulty in stating it in the Estimates for the information of the House, but in this case I see the difficulty of putting in any particular amount. It is not intended by the law that there shall be a limit to the amount in this case, and as there is no fixed sum it would not be easy to state it in the Estimates each year as the member for Dorchester desires. However, the main point taken by the member for Dorchester is correct: that the minister has no authority to spend one dollar unless it has been first voted by the House. All these sums mentioned as authorized by statute have ben voted by the House; otherwise there would be no authority for spending them. But I agree with the minister that it is not necessary in all cases to set the amounts out in detail; in cases where there is not a fixed sum he might have difficulty, indeed, in doing so.
I submit there is no more difficulty in fixing the amount in this item than there was in fixing it in the next item of $26,000 for a bounty on linen yarn.
I believe that is not voted by statute. It is done by an Order in Council, and unless it is voted by this House from year to year, it cannot be paid at all.
I contend that this item should not be paid either.
That is another question.

The minister this afternoon said that the statute was passed by the Liberal administration. If it had any usefulness at the time, apparently its usefulness has passed, and surely the minister should not attempt to perpetuate any evil legislation on the part of the former Liberal administration as an excuse for fur-

ther expenditure of this nature. If the expenditure is unnecessary-and I think it is; indeed I do not think the principle of bounties is good in any event-why not eliminate it? Is it not time that the Government should look around for ways and means of saving money instead of spending it in every possible way? To be consistent, the Government should either eliminate this bounty or throw the lands open for prospecting to all. The Government is adopting a principle of paying a bounty to one set of people and not giving other people an opportunity of prospecting. The person who has a little oil well is getting his bounty, but the Government does not allow others to go in and prospect. The fact that this appropriation has been passed from year to year, is not a sufficient excuse for its continuance. There must be some period at which this bounty will terminate, and I do not think it was the intention of the Government of that day to perpetuate it. If there is no advantage in continuing it this year, why not discontinue it? The Government never seem to find any way by which they can save money; with them, it is always a question of added expenditure. The only excuse they offer is: Well, this legislation was passed by a Liberal administration; therefore, it must be good. I am quite free to admit that about the only good things they have to offer are some of the things which they have taken from the Liberal administration, but I do not think this is one of them and it should be eliminated at once.

I cannot follow the argument of my hon. friend. As I understand the matter, this is a bonus which was given to oil producers in counties of southwest-era Ontario where the production is so low as to make it almost impossible to proceed with that production unless some Government assistance is furnished. That was the situation at the time the Act was passed under the late Liberal administration, and it is much more the position today, because from that time the production of individual wells in those counties has gradually and continually decreased. What I rose to speak about is this. I wish to take the minister back to the statement he made a short time ago when he said that this bounty is limited to oil of a certain specific gravity. I think he threw out the suggestion-I do not think it was more

than that-that this was done because this may have coincided with the specific gravity of oil which must necessarily be imported to meet our domestic needs in this country. I do not know whether or not that was the fact at that time. My view is that this has always been an incentive to the production, discovery and exploration of oil in this country. In Alberta, we have a grade of oil which is very different in specific gravity from oil obtained in Ontario, and to that Alberta oil this bounty is not applicable. In Ontario, the wells are sunk to a depth of only 400 to 1,000 feet at a very small cost, whereas in Alberta, wells are sunk to a depth of some three or four thousand feet, it costing $40,000 to $100,000 to put down one well. The quantities of oil which we have been obtaining southwest of Calgary are no't great although the value of the oil-is great, and the field may have potentialities. I wish to point out the unfairness of paying a bounty in Ontario where the cost of obtaining oil is so small, when a bounty is not paid to those who produce oil in Alberta where very great cost is incurred in putting down wells. I think this matter has already been presented to the minister in petitions, and he has probably looked carefully into the matter and will have an answer ready. The bounty should be continued until such time as we discover in Canada the sort of oil which will enable us to produce oil in competition with the outside world on an equal basis without the necessity of a bounty. Until that time a bounty should be paid by this Government, not only to assist those who are now producing, but to encourage others to explore and prospect for oil, the necessity for which in this country no one can dispute.

I have listened with
great interest to the remarks contributed to the committee by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), who has had a long experience in this House as Minister of Finance and as a member. His opinions have great weight and I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce will not dispute the opinion given by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. But the two hon. gentlemen seem to agree on one point, and that point is that statutory expenditure has not to be voted by Parliament every year. I accept with great respect their opinion; but on
90 i
the other hand I would submit that the wording of the Estimates and also the spirit of the law, as I understand it, although I may be wrong, do not seem to agree with that opinion. I would refer the minister to page 4 of the Estimates, on which there is a summary of the whole expenditure for the current year? What do we read? It is the "summary of the estimated expenditure of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1922, together with the sums granted for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1921"-that is granted not, for an indefinite period, but for a definite period- "and a statement showing the increase and decrease for each service." If we read the summary in one column, we see the ordinary Estimates and in the other column we see the Estimates authorised by Statute. The law was passed in Parliament in 1904, says my right hon. friend. This law, having been enacted by Parliament, and having been sanctioned by the Governor General, becomes the law of Canada. That sanction is an authority to the Government to put the law into force, and one of the provisions of the law is that moneys are to be expended. I say that as far as the money part of the law is concerned, it has to be placed before Parliament every year in just the same way as every statutory vote is placed in the Estimates for all the departments. Being placed before Parliament in that way, which is not as formal and direct a way as is followed in the case of the other Estimates, every year Parliament gives a new authority to the Government to expend the sum which is mentioned in the law, and my contention is that unless this is done the Government has not the authority to spend the money. I do not wish to detain the committee very much longer on this point, but I might recall to the right hon. gentleman that in the old days in England when Parliament met only at long intervals, perhaps once in 15 or 25 years at the convenience of the King, the King did not need Parliament because at the opening of each reign Parliament met and voted once for all what was called the civil list and that civil list covered the expenditure for the whole administration of the realm during the reign of that sovereign. That was changed at the Revolution, and after 1688 the law was laid down by the British Parliament that in future moneys would be voted for only 12 months, and would be voted only after an itemized and detailed account had been submitted to

Parliament. Therefore I say that my contention is correct, and that my right hon. friend has no right, any more than has any other member of the Government, to spend a dollar of public money unless it has first been voted by Parliament. If my right hon. friend will refer to page 2 of the summary he will find that it does not contain one single cent of expenditure by his department authorized by statute. The position taken by the right hon. gentleman to-night might be improved if he would give more information to the committee; if he would tell us approximately what amount of money is to be expended this year in bounties to petroleum companies, and if he would do what all his other colleagues have done-place in the Estimates the moneys authorized by Parliament. I appreciate what my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's has pointed out, that it is very hard to fix a precise amount, but this law has been in force since 1904; the officials of the department know how it works, they are acquainted with all these companies and have a good idea as to the quantities of oil produced each year; so I think the official whose salary we are voting now should be in a position to give sufficient information to the minister to enable him to do with regard to his department what his colleagues all do with regard to theirs. I would ask another question of my right hon. friend. According to the law which was passed in 1904, is the amount to be expended by his department limited?
It is one-and-a-half cents per gallon for every gallon of oil which comes up to the test.

Suppose these new oil
fields which have been discovered in the West produce immense quantities of oil. Does my right hon. friend contend that, without giving any figures to the committee, or any more information that than he has done, he has authorization by this Parliament to give out in bounties at the rate of one-and-a-half cents per gallon, millions and millions of dollars? Where would he stop? We do not know. According to his interpretion of the law there is no limit to the amount he can expend. If that is the case, next year when we come back, if we do come back, and ask the right hon. gentleman how much money was expended, and he answers that in consequence of the immense success of these new oil fields he has paid, out in bounties ten to fifteen million dollars, we could not be able to reproach him in any way, unless we now 	,
insist upon his giving us more information and fixing a limit, so that we shall know where we are going. I think the right hon. gentleman will acknowledge that the position I am taking is very reasonable. We cannot give to his department a blank cheque any more than we can to any other department, and we have all the more reason for not doing so because he does not mention anywhere in his Estimates the amount which he is to expend, either as authorized by Parliament or otherwise. In the summary it is stated that the expenditure authorized by statute for the year 1921-22 amounts to $114,000,000, and then the total amount of the other Estimates is given, but in neither of these two columns does this particular expenditure appear. I do not think it is reasonable for the right hon. gentleman to insist on the committee giving him an absolutely blank cheque for this expenditure.

I do not know that there is much to be gained by prolonging the discussion between my hon. friend and myself. The position I take I am quite willing to let go before the House, and the House can judge of it. The ex-minister of Finance, and trusted leader of my hon. friend, has coincided absolutely with my view.
And also with mine.

May I ask my hon. friend if when he made the statement that the minister could not spend a single dollar except it was voted by this chamber, he included in that assertion the vote of money by statute, or was he referring only to the annual votes which we pass here?

My statement was to
the effect that all moneys to be expended by the Government must first be voted by Parliament.

My hon. friend said that I could not spend anything during the next year except it had been voted by the House this year. There my hon. friend and myself differ entirely, and my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance agrees with me absolutely. No one in this House believes that any minister has the right to spend money unless it is either voted in the Estimates or provided by statute, but the statute may provide for expenditure for years and years and years, and we never revote in the House what Parliament has already voted through a law which it has passed.
