My hon. friend says that if my officer were really any good he ought to give me such information as would enable me to put the precise sum in the Estimates. How can you do that? My hon. friend must realize that although you have the records to go by you can put in the Estimates only approximately what the cost will be. The production differs from year to year. Some years it is twice what it was the year before, and sometimes you will find a falling off of 50 per cent in production in the course of a year. So that it would be altogether misleading to attempt to put before the committee an exact estimate of what you would spend. You must put a sufficient amount to keep you out of all difficulties, even though it might not all be used. Every member has the Auditor General's report, which is a treasured document, and he knows exactly what is spent each year. That is, therefore, a guide. Now, with reference to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Griesbach), I have had many communications from the West regarding oil fields producing oil that does not fulfil the test that is required before the bounty is payable. This is a vexed question, and in one way it seems to be unfair. But you have only to go back to the purpose for which this bounty was given, namely, to compensate for legislation that was passed some time ago, equalizing the quality of oil produced here with that imported from the United States, in order to get at the basis of the matter. The proposition is put up to me strongly: why not change the law so that it will cover our oil-producing regions in the West? Well, frankly, the question then would be as to where we should land if we made the subsidy applicable to all oil produced in Canada; and should the promises of large production in the West, which at present seem to be very great, be realized, it would involve a very heavy charge upon the revenues of the country. This specific gravity test has been on the statute books for quite a while, and I am not going to say that because it has been there it should remain there for ever. It is a matter for the House to take into consideration if it thinks that the time has come when that provision ought to be done away with; and there are different minds with reference to that. But until there is a change in the law, it is, of course, my duty to administer the Act as I find it. With reference to the millions upon millions which I might find myself under the necessity of spending, if something on a large scale took place in the North West -well, if we proceed on suppositions I fear
we may get off the solid basis of argument. I do not look for any such expansion. Anyway, so far, the specific gravity test has been the differentiating factor in the granting of the bounty.

I want to say a word or two, not in connection with the discussion that has taken place, although I think the country and the House should be thankful to my hon. friend (Mr. Cannon) for having put his point so clearly, that is to say, that not a dollar should be spent without the authority of Parliament.
That has been long recognized.
Yes; but the sooner it is made clear in the Estimates as to what our statutory expenditures are, the sooner those expenditures are specifically stated, the better it will be.
That might be.

We are facing a very
[DOT] serious situation and the country is entitled to know what expenditures are to be made every year. The public will be more and more critical also in regard to the total amount of our expenditures. Although theoretically, on one branch of the argument, my right hon. friend is correct, yet the hon. member for Dorchester has rendered the country a service this evening in calling the attention of the committee to this very important question of putting before the country the real expenditures which are to be made and which are proper only as sanctioned by Parliament. The point I wish to make, however, is this: We are paying a bounty on the production of crude petroleum. I remember when this bounty was created by Parliament; as my right hon. friend stated a moment ago, it was in the year 1904. Now, I am not going to suggest the creating of other bounties, because I do not think that the country at the present time is in a mood to grant further subsidies. But in connection with oil, would it not be possible to encourage the exploitations of the large fields of shale oil in my right hon. friend's native province as well as in my own? There are immense fields of shale oil in the province of New Brunswick, in the county of Albert; and lately very large fields of shale oil have been discovered in the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure. As I say, I am not asking for a bounty, nor would I dare propose the creation of one for the development of those fields. But when the new tariff is enacted, the Government should help the

pioneers and the miners by decreasing or completely abolishing the duties on the machinery needed by the miners and operators for the development of those fields of shale oil. I believe I am speaking by the book when I say that my right hon. friend, who is familiar with this question, has reason to view this suggestion with sympathy, not only because it concerns his own province or the east of Canada, but because the whole subject is a highly important one. This country is in need of fuel oil, and the Government should help to develop these natural resources. Evidence was taken by a committee which sat a year or so ago in the Senate chambers, where experts were heard, and it was recognized and admitted that these fields of shale oil can be successfully developed if the Government will agree to admit the necessary machinery without exacting the duties that are at present levied. In all mining ventures, and especially in regard to oil, the crucial test, or, to use Wilsonian language, the acid test, is the period of development; and if the miner or the operator cannot secure at reasonable rates the machinery and the engineering required for that development, he is, of course, barred out, and under such circumstances these fields will remain unproductive. I call the attention of the right hon. gentleman to that fact. We-I should not say "we", because I am not .the owner of any of these fields, but the Canadian people-would be pleased if the Government would give free machinery, and free mining implements, in order to promote the development and the operation of those natural resources.

I want to ask the right hon. gentleman a simple question touching a matter as to which I would like to be enlightened. We read on page 4 of the Estimates that the grand total of the expenditure for the next year will be $582,000,000. Does that represent the whole of the expenditure for next year barring the Supplementary Estimates?
My hon. friend's question has reference to the figures in the third column?

Yes. The grand total of the summary is $582,000,000. If we have no Supplementary Estimates this session does this amount represent the whole of the money that will be paid out during the next fiscal year?

I would not
undertake to say that it does. That third

column is the total of the two sums in the two preceding columns, of what is to be voted and what is authorized by statute, but whether everything authorized by statute is included in that amount or not I do not know. If it is, then that would represent the total amount that could be paid out, exclusive of expenditures by Governor General's warrant for special emergencies and things of that nature.

May I further ask whether the minister expects that during the next fiscal year his department will pay out about the same amount as that which appears in the Auditor General's Report for the last fiscal year in bounties on crude petroleum? The figure for the year ended March 31, 1920, was $103,000. Does the right hon. gentleman think that the amount to be paid out during the present fiscal year will exceed that sum or be about the same?

There again I cannot give a definite answer. In one year
350,000	gallons of oil are raised; in another year the quantity is 202,000 gallons. What is raised one year is no definite lead as to what may be raised the succeeding year. Last year a certain number of gallons were raised, and the bounty was paid on that quantity at the rate which is allowed. Next year there may be half that amount raised, or there may be fifty per cent more than that raised-it is impossible to say. That indefinite feature is there and you cannot get over it; you can make no definite statement with regard to it, From the year 1904 that item has never appeared, so far as I know, in the "Authorized by law column" of the Estimates. I suppose the reason it is not put in is that you would be rather misleading the House if you put in a certain amount not knowing whether the production of oil would rise or would fall, or would remain just about the same.

Where you are dealing with a contract for the construction of a work by the Government, or anything of that kind which is under government control, you can, through your officers, make a reasonable estimate of what you are going to do-
Yes.
-but when you are dealing with corporations over whom you have no control-
And with Providence.

-you cannot make an estimate with any accuracy; you have to be dependent upon the work '	10 p.m. which it suits their convenience
to do. Now, in fairness, while we are on this branch of the subject I must say that we have in times past spent vast sums under the authority of statutes which have not appeared in the Estimates. Let me take as an illustration the railway subsidies. Again and again we have voted railway subsidies and millions-many millions-of dollars have been expended under these Acts, but my recollection is that they never in any case appeared in the Estimates. Let me mention another case. Within my own experience we have spent millions in bounties on steel and iron, and I do not recall any case in which they were mentioned in the Estimates. Why? For the reason I have just given, that they were not Government works; they were operations carried on by corporations over whom the Government had no control; and so long as there was statutory authority to pay the money-at any rate, speaking within my own recollection-I do not think it was customary to mention these sums in the Estimates. I agree that it would be a convenience if you could have a general summing up of the whole thing, but in the case of the operations carried on by corporations that would have to be largely a matter of guess work.

We may at all events draw the conclusion that the amounts specified in the main Estimates do not cover the whole expenditure for next year, and it is a disagreeable revelation that at least $100,000 can be added to the already very large sum required for the next fiscal year without the public knowing anything about it.

May I make a suggestion? I think most of the people who take an interest in these matters have been accustomed to feel, though quite wrongly, that the sum total found at the beginning of the Estimates was the amount which the country would have to provide for the fiscal year next ensuing. Now we learn that they are amounts authorized by statute which do not appear in the summary. The fact that some of these amounts do appear in the summary would lead the ordinary reader to suppose that all expenditures authorized by statute do find a place there. In order that the public, who, though they have not taken an interest in the past in our financial condition, are bound to do so in the future, may have a more correct idea of just what the commitments of the country are, I would make this suggestion, which I trust is a reasonable one-that there should appear at the end of the summary a statement of what was paid under the authority of statute which is not mentioned in the summary itself. I quite understand from the statements of the minister and the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) that it may be quite difficult to estimate the amounts that are to be paid under any special statute, by way of bounties, for instance; but we [DOT]should be able to put in a supplementary statement at the end of the summary showing what has been paid under the authority of statutes for the preceding year.
For the last year?
Yes, for the last year.
You find that in the Auditor General's report.

No doubt all these things are available if one knows just where to look for them, either in the Auditor General's report or in the Public Accounts; but my suggestion is that when persons- members of this House and the outside public who are interested in these matters -come to examine the Estimates, they should have before them in convenient form exactly what is submitted to the House and voted, and what was paid under statute, although difficult of computation, for the past year.

The minister seems to
take the position that the principle of bounties cannot fairly be discussed in connection with this item. In a sense he is perhaps correct, yet I would like to associate myself with the member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) in his opposition to the granting of bounties. I have not heard the minister give any reason whatever why these bounties should continue to be paid, except that they are paid under a statute enacted in 1904. With all respect to the right hon. gentleman, I do not think that is a sufficient reason for their continuance. This matter is directly in his department, and it seems to me that he should proceed

on the principle that the monies to be paid out by way of bounties are for some definite purpose. If he believes the reasons which moved the previous government to give these bounties by way of encouraging oil production still hold good, he should be prepared to defend those reasons. I am entirely opposed to bounties and I think it is time to repeal the law under which they were granted. I question very much whether the bounty of a cent and a half a gallon encourages the production of oil; it merely adds that much more to the profits of those who do not require any assistance. Unless the minister is convinced that the granting of bounties does still give encouragement to oil production, I think he ought seriously to consider the introduction of legislation to repeal the Act under which these bounties were first granted.	.

As the Supplementary
Estimates are sometimes laid on the table of the House as late as the end of June, would it not be well to include in them the amount paid during the fiscal year ended the previous March, so that the country will know exactly the amount likely to be paid during the current year? I would ask the right hon. gentleman to bring this suggestion to the attention of his colleagues.
I will.

I am sure my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) must be impressed with the strength of sentiment opposed to the principle of bounties. The words which have just gone from my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) are very impressive. I have no doubt myself that this item, small as it is, is a waste of public money. I settled that question for myself many years ago, and when I first came to this House I expressed myself more than once along those lines. I think my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) has pointed out to the minister a more excellent way of helping the exploration of the wealth beneath the surface of the earth-by making it easier to get the implements by which that wealth may be won. I have not had time to look into what the Argentine has done of recent years, but before the war she had no duty whatever on mining implements, and the Argentine resembles Canada in these respects, that it is thinly populated and is a new country. My right hon. friend balks at the idea of paying out this bounty on large amounts of oil; but he contends for this modest sum of $3,000. That attitude brings him to what is the fundamental and,

in my opinion, the insurmountable objection to bounties. You can only pay a bounty to two kinds of business: either to a business which is a paying business, when obviously it does not need any assistance and it is a gross injustice to the taxpayers to assist it; or to a non-paying business, which is a foolish waste of public money. In the ab- [DOT] sence of bounties people would put their capital and their energies into a line of business which on the whole was likely to be remunerative; otherwise, they would withdraw from it. I hope my right hon. friend has been impressed, as I have been, with the strength of sentiment that has been expressed by my hon. friends from Dorchester, Pontiac, Maisonneuve and other hon. gentlemen. I want to add my modest word to theirs, and I hope if he does bring in the Estimates another year he will be so much impressed by the arguments advanced to-night that he will drop even this small sum. I want to reiterate in a sentence that, in my humble judgment, it is a waste of public money, and certainly no responsible citizen of Canada at the present time will argue for one moment that we have any money to waste.

My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Redman) states that this bounty is necessary for wells that are not producing enough oil to make them pay for the labour expended on them, but he must know that such enterprises are better closed down at once. He might just as well argue that his friend who is sitting beside him, the member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), would be justified in asking for a bounty on fish in portions of Lake Superior which have been fished out.
I have no doubt that the right hon. gentleman would grant such a bounty, and I also have no doubt that lots of fishermen would be ready to take that bounty to catch fish.
They would catch the bounty.

Yes, that is what most of them are looking for. The principle of bounties is wrong. When an enterprise will not pay for the labour, and we have too many remunerative occupations for our people to waste their time and money on those that are unprofitable. The minister has stated that if it was the wish of Parliament to abolish this bounty, it would be abolished. I am quite satisfied that if I moved to strike the item out the minister would call to his support all his followers, and the item would carry. Legislation is conducted by the Government, and the Gov-

ernment is sure of the votes of its supporters. While they may criticise, as they did this afternoon, when it comes to a vote they are sure to support the ministry. Therefore such a suggestion cannot come from this side with any hope of success; at least, the amendments we have made so far have been voted down. The time is coming, and coming soon, when that will not be the case. But in the meantime what can Parliament do about it? It is for the minister to take the responsibility for this expenditure, and before he asks for an unlimited amount, say $100,000 or $200,000, he should consider well the advisability of eliminating unnecessary expenditure. This is not a time for unnecessary expenditure.

Before this item is passed I wish again to protest against the principle of giving bounties to companies and corporations that do not need them. I object also to our voting a salary to an official who will distribute an amount which is nowhere mentioned in the Estimates. In other words, we are giving a blank cheque to the Department of Trade and Commerce and my right hon. friend can spend any amount he wishes; there is nothing to restrict or to curb his extravagance if he is inclined to be extravagant. If my right hon. friend's contention is correct that if an expenditure is authorized by statute he does not have to come back to the House and have the amount voted but can spend what he likes each year, the Government might as well introduce a Bill conferring upon themselves the power to spend a lump sum of say $500,000,000. We would then have no budget; the usefulness of the House of Commons would disappear, and the Government would be able to run the country as they wish to run it.

Item agreed to.
Canada Year Book, $20,000.
What is the reason for the increase?
It is due largely to the increase in the cost of paper.
How many of these books are distributed free, and what good purpose is served by spending $20,000 for the Year Book? Is it worth the money to the people, and if so, in what way?

That might be a debatable question; it would depend upon one's point of view. I, myself, have no doubt as to the utility of the book and the usefulness of the purpose which it
serves. I know of no progressive country in the world which does not publish a year book of singular excellence. Our year book has been published for a number of years; its quality and efficacy, so to speak, have been increasing each year and I believe that Canada has to-day, with the possible exception of Australia, a year book as comprehensive, as well put up, and as consecutive in the information which it gives as that of any other country which publishes such a book. Last year we published an English edition of about
9.000	copies and a French edition of about
3.000	copies at a cost of $22,000. The work is now done in the Printing Bureau; formerly that was not the case. A certain number of copies are distributed to libraries, chambers of commerce, and permanent institutions of that kind, where they are available to those who seek information concerning Canada. Then, a price, which is just about the cost of publication, is charged for all copies distributed, other than the complimentary copies of which I have spoken. One feature which has been introduced in the book is, I think, valuable. Each year an exhaustive article is published dealing with one particular phase of Canada's development-whether concerning her history, her mineral wealth, or otherwise-so as to bring up to date all the information in compendious form with reference to that subject. Then in succeeding publications there is a reference column to articles which appeared in the preceding books, so that if one does not find in this year's book the information which he seeks he may refer to the previous volume dealing with the subject.
How many have been distributed each year?
I cannot tell my hon. friend the number, but I can get the information for him.
The information in the book covers the calendar year?
Yes.
I have noticed that the Canadian Almanac contains more recent information in some respects than that which appears in the Canada Year Book.

Yes, that is bound to be the case. The Year Book is not so much a pocket volume containing strictly up-to-date information as a permanent record. It takes a good deal of time to prepare it and get it published.
Has the Year Book always been published under the name "Canada Year Book," or was there some other title?
I think the earlier volumes had a different name, but it has had the name "Canada Year Book" for a number of years.
The Imperial Canadian Year Book is a different publication?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Culling timber, including an amount of $600 for superannuated cullers, $1,600.
Why have we to pay cullers? I did not know the Government was in the timber busines.

This comes in as the tail end of a long transaction, and this is the last time it will appear. It has been gradually diminished by appointments not being made, until I think we have now three officers left who are being paid small superannuations. Most of them, I regret to say, are over eighty years of age and will soon disappear. The active operations of this work will disappear after this year.

Item agreed to.
Grant to Canadian Engineering' Standards Association for the promotion of uniformity of standards in metallic and other products, ?iC,000.
' Mr. CAHILL: What does this appropriation accomplish?

This appropriation has appeared for the last two or three years, and when the committee understands what it is for, I am sure it will consider the apropriation a very useful one. It is granted to the Canadian Engineering Standards Association. The Canadian Engineers banded themselves together, and they are now at work particularly in forming standards of various kinds, so as to standardize productive operations. As members of the association they give their whole time to this work, and we give them a grant of $10,000 to enable them to carry on.
Are they meeting with any positive success?

Yes. They have divided themselves into a large number of committees, each committee taking up one special subject with the idea of introducing standardization in regard to that

product, whatever it is. They get together and canvass the question, discuss the standards that they fix, come to an agreement and then bring all the pressure they can to bear upon the manufacturing companies to adopt those standards. They are meeting with great success in that respect. Anyone who will think for a moment will realize the great economic gain which would be had if, instead of a manufacturer devoting himself to five, six, seven, eight or ten different standards in the manufacture of an article of use, he could bring those down to the minimum number of usable standards and manufacture along that line.
Do they make reports to the Department?

Yes, and we
have on record the results of their work.
Are the reports available for the public?

We have them on record; we have not printed them. My hon. friend could get any in which he is interested.
Honorary Advisory Council of Industrial and Scientific Research,-salaries and expenses, including printing and stationery and the collection and distribution of information, and for studentships, scholarships, special problems and forestry studies, $120,000.

In the speech from the
Throne reference is made to a Bill dealing with scientific research. Will any expenditure entailed by that Bill be in addition to this amount, or does this include it?

This does not
include it. What is contemplated in that allusion is something of a much more extended kind; it is really a national laboratory for standardization and research. On the other hand, this would have an intimate connection therewith, and when the other is established, this would work in with it to a very large extent. That correlation would have to be made after we knew the form of the new venture, so to speak.
The latter part of the item refers to: "forestry studies." Is that work in a forestry products laboratory?

That is an
explanation, a little more extended, of what is meant by the research. Those are the lines along which they are carrying on research. They include not only the research and salaries and expenses, but a system of studentships, fellowships

and bursaries which the advisory council supervise, and, after proper examination, award for special researches in different lines. They take up quite a large range at the present time. There are included in them some forestry problems, mining problems, productive problems in industry, and scientific problems to a certain extent where they are trying to solve difficulties which are met in processes of production and they carry on experiments to that end. the system of bursaries, fellowships and studentships has been found to work well in Great Gritain and other countries, and the same line is being followed out under this research board.

I would venture the
assertion that the work conducted under this Advisory Council of Industrial and Scientific Research might far better be conducted under the universities of this country. For instance, we know that in the Faculty of Applied Science of McGill Universities we have had some of the leading scientists, I may say, of the whole world, some men who occupy chairs in that faculty are really men of world-wide reputation and have done a great deal of their most important work in connection with the university. What I am afraid of, in voting this $120,000, is that we are largely duplicating the work of the universities, and I think if we wish to promote scientific and industrial research, that work can much better be carried on in the great scientific schools attached to universities like McGill, Toronto Varsity and Queen's University at Kingston.

The University of
Montreal.

The University of
Monereal, Laval University and others. I would like to bring forward this objection which, I believe, is a serious one. Would the minister inform us how he expects with the appliances available at Ottawa to have the work done as well as it would be done with the magnificant equipment at McGill, for instance, and I speak of McGill not because I do not realize there are other universities splendidly equipped, but because I am familiar with the equipment of my Alma Mater.

I am afraid my hon. friend has not read the yearly reports as diligently as he might have done if he had had more time. The universities are not ignored under this system. Their energies are co-ordinated by the members of the Research Council, many of whom
are connected with the universities. These researches are not carried on by means of appliances here in Ottawa, but at the universities themselves by members of the universities, either professors or students who have gained their degrees or passed through most of their courses and have specialized in some one of the subjects. They are appointed under the bursary studentship and fellowship appropriations to carry on during the vacation months researches along a certain line. Here is a research, for instance, being carried on by Professor Porter of McGill University. A grant of $1,500 is proposed to be given him out of this vote in order to defray his expenses in carrying on an investigation with reference to oil flotation in the recovery of values, by the application of Canadian and other oils, taking into consideration minerals other than those of the Cobalt district. There is a line along which iesearch has been extended. The professor has been at work on that and shows an aptitude for it. This grant is given to him under the supervision of the Research Council to enable him to defray his expenses in carrying on that investigation for another year. That is just an example of how the work is done. There is no laboratory here under the management of the Research Council where independent research is undertaken. I have a number of instances here of bursaries, studentships, fellowships, and grants for researches that are being carried on at McGill, Queen's, Toronto University, and other universities which have the appliances and the skilled workmanship necessary to enable them to undertake that work.

I would not like the minister to think I was opposed to research work. I am glad to know that it is being carried on in these places where it can best be carried on, but I would like to be convinced of the necessity for this council in regard to this work. Would the minister tell us roughly how much of this $120,000 is going to the actual work of research at the universities, a'nd how much goes for the salaries of officers or officials connected with the council?

The Research Council is composed of a number of gentlemen who are selected because of professional and scientific knowledge and skill, also of men who are versed in and familiar with the industries of the country. All of them give their services without any

remuneration with the exception of the president, who is a constant or stationary officer and who had to give up his work in the university and become a sort of Director for the Research Council, supervising their work. All the others give their services free. We pay their expenses when they come to Ottawa for their meetings, which are every fortnight or three weeks as necessity dictates. Dr. Macallum, who was the Director, and received a salary of $10,000, has resigned and gone on a mission to Pekin after being appointed to a position in McGill University. His place has been taken by Dr. Ruttan, who is filling the position until we come to a conclusion in reference to the laboratory which has been spoken about and the rearrangements which are to be made. He fills that position gratuitously. I make that explanation to show that salaries are not a large part of the expenditure. The others receive their travelling expenses and their living allowances when they are attending the meetings. Last year, salaries and allowances and the staff which is necessary to carry on the work consumed $14,800, printing and stationery and travelling expenses of members took up a certain amount and the standard gauge laboratory equipment took up $9,000. I must make an explanation with reference to the standard gauge laboratory equipment. It had been purchased by the Imperial Munitions Board, and had been used by them to a certain extent. When the Imperial Munitions Board was demobilized this valuable machinery remained there. The value of it was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30,000. They offered it to the Research Council for $9,000. It is worth fully the amount that I stated first. After consultation, the Research Council decided to buy it at $9,000. It could be sold at more than that price at any time, but if thi.s new arrangement is made and comes into force it will be absolutely necessary to have that gauge. Forestry examinations took $8,000, assistant researches, seventeen in all, $24,467, fellowships $4,100, studentships $4,125, and bursaries $2,150.
Are all these studentships carried in Canada?	.
All in Canada.
None in England?

No. Professor McLennan, who has charge of the physics laboratory in Toronto, has been conducting

experiments there for us. During the war, he was taken over to England and employed by the British Government in research work, and his investigations proved very valuable indeed. While in England he was working for the British Government, not for us.

How many of these
students are there?

There were
seventeen researches carried on last year in different lines, an example of one of which I put before the House. There are six students.

Are they university
graduates?

They are university graduates or undergraduates who have made their mark and shown a distinct aptitude in and desire for a certain line of research, and they are selected by the Research Council after consultation with the presidents of the universities with a view to obtaining the best men. They are given fellowships which enable them to carry on research.

In glancing over the
Auditor General's report, I would submit, for the consideration of the minister, that the overhead, if I may so term it, in connection with this enterprise, is very much higher than it should be. The administrative chairman is far from being a stationary officer, for I see he spent seventy-eight and three-quarters days at $10 per day travelling around, and his railways fares amounted to about $436. The expenses in connection with this undertaking amount to about $33,000 out of a total of some $94,000 for the work that is supposed to be done. I think the thing is top-heavy, and there are comparatively few students who are being helped. At any rate, the amount spent on helping students is very much less than the overhead. Let me draw the attention of the committee to this item:
Dr. Andrew Hunter, Toronto: Grant to aid in research into the problems of the fox-breeding industry, honorarium $200, travelling expenses, $191.10, advance for expenses, $5,000.
I respectfully submit that if you are going to make experiments in fox breeding, an amount to some fox breeder down in Prince Edward Island would be a good deal wiser than grants to any gentlemen who lives in Toronto. I never knew that city to be famous for fox production.
They have to be foxy.

It strikes me that
we have paid out a good deal of public money in this direction, and far too much has gone in the way of expenses to those who were not doing the real work, but who were more or less supervising. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization has a very wise look on his face and perhaps he could give us some information in regard to the subject of fox breeding. I throw out this suggestion because there is a sapient expression on his face.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of
the subject.

First, with
reference to over-head expenses. The one purpose of the Research Council was to interest scientific bodies and to line them up as far as possible in accordant action. In order to do that they must visit the different parts of the Dominion and consult with those men and form organizations. To have said to Dr. Macallum, "We will pay you $10,000 as director, and then make you stay in Ottawa so as to obviate travelling expenses", would not have been a proper manner in which to conduct the enterprise. Dr. Macallum did travel over every part of the Dominion. He called on scientific and university men, had conversations and conferences with them, and formed them into groups which affiliated themselves in woi'k with the Advisory Council, under their direction. That was the first really excellent step that was taken. It had to be taken if you were going to collect information, focus scientific research work in Canada, and carry it on under proper supervision and in a regular manner. With reference to fox breeding, this is an industry that has had its ups and downs. On the whole it has shown possibilities of very large returns, not only from foxes, but from other wild animals that might be cultivated. The difficulties in fox culture arise, so far as I understand, chiefly in regard to habitat, feeding, and procreation of foxes. Foxes are, of course, a foxy lot, and many a breeder, after he has spent large sums of money, and has obtained a litter, suddenly finds, after leaving them in good condition one day, that the next day they have in some way or other disappeared. Very frequently they are destroyed by the mother herself. Now why is that? The mother fox destroys her young through fright. Some clumsy method in dealing with these animals may give rise to fright on the part of the mother and she probably thinks that
the best way of standing between them and their enemies is by destroying them. An endeavour is made to provide proper food and, generally, such treatment as will make the habitat as natural as possible and on the whole make for natural conditions. This research work was carried on in the actual farming! of foxes for a certain period. Strict scientific observation was made of them on which conclusions might be based as to the best methods of feeding,, breeding and looking after them. When that information is ascertained, and has behind it scientific authority, as well as experience, it will prove very valuable to the fox breeding industry as a whole.
What is Dr. Andrew Hunter, who is devoting his attention to fox breeding? Is he a veterinary doctor?
So far as this research goes, I suppose you would call him a fox doctor.
Well, he is doctoring foxes and he gets an advance for expenses of $5,000.

That is for
carrying on experiments.
Where has he carried on these experiments?

In Prince
Edward Island in the vicinity of Ottawa.

Well, I submit that it is not wise to appoint a man who is a veterinary doctor, or a homeopather, or a dentist, who lives in Toronto, to carry on investigations of this nature in Prince Edward Island. Why should a man in Toronto be engaged to carry on research work in Prince Edward Island at a total expenditure last year of over $5,000?

I am not a fox doctor, nor am I an authority on the breeding of animals. My hon. friend, however, has a high opinion of McGill University, and I know he has an equally high opinion of Dr. Ruttan who was on the Advisory Council, which thought it necessary, after a thorough consideration of the matter, to devote a certain amount of money to this purpose. He was one of the Advisory Council who made that proposal. I cannot give my hon. friend the information which I know he could obtain from Dr. Ruttan, although I could get it for him and give him a memorandum on the subject. I know ij: would be both interesting and

instructive as well as satisfactory to my hon. friend if he would meet Dr. Ruttan and talk the matter over with him.

There are many things which we should like to do in Canada if we had the money. I do submit, with all -respect to the minister, that the country's finances are not such as to warrant the expenditure of this amount of money on investigating the psychology of mother foxes in order to provide some remedy against their unnatural and most unmotherly propensity for dining off their young. As a matter of fact, the member for Cha-teauguay and Huntingdon (Mr. Robb), who has experience in country life and is member for one of the finest agricultural counties in the Dominion, tells me that the female pig also very often does the same thing. To my mind, Mr. Chairman, we have to economize, and I think the Government is very severely to blame for spending so much money on this sort of scientific investigation.

It is not only scientific, but it is practical. This industry is one which is largely carried on at the present time -and is capable of almost indefinite expansion in our country. I will just read a little memorandum I have on the subject for the benefit of my hon. friend:
To the Associate Committee of the Research Council investigating the problems affecting the fox-breeding industry of the Dominion.
I may say that $5,500 was the grant.
This committee has been engaged for over a year in studying the causation of the' low yield from this industry. In Prince Edward Island the average number of fox pups to a litter ranges from three to five, but the number of pups reared to maturity averages only one to three per pair of foxes. The loss, therefore, is in the neighborhood of about sixty-five per cent of each litter, and apparently is largely due to wholly unsuitable diet which affects the mother vixen before the birth of the litter, and also the young pups. There is no knowledge for the fox breeders to go upon on this score, and the Fox-Breeders' Association appealed, over a year and a half ago, to have this investigation conducted under the auspices of the Research Council. This was agreed to by the latter, which planned an investigation which would extend over two years at least. The associate committee consists of five professors-
Now I will catch my hon. friend-'
-of biochemistry and physiology two representatives of the Department of Agriculture, one of whom is Dr. Tjorrance, the Veterinary Director General of the Health of Animals Branch. The investigation is now being conducted under the auspices of the Associate Committee by an expert Canadian biochemist, who

has, for the past fifteen years, been engaged in studying the nutrition of farm animals in the North Western States and Canada, and who has control of part of the Research Laboratory of the Health of Animals Branch at Hull, P.Q., where there are installed special pens for the foxes and special equipment in the laboratory for this purpose, at the expense of the Department of Agriculture.
The Fox Breeders' Association have donated six pair of foxes estimated at a value of $2,000, which are now under observation as to diet and the resulting state of nourishment. Already data have been obtained which seem to point the way to a standard diet for these animals which, if established, will lower the mortality amongst the young foxes and thus save, it is hoped, about a million dollars a year for Prince Edward Island alone.
The grant will enable the work to be continued until the end of 1921.
Are the grants made by the minister or by the Council?

The grants are recommended by the Council and the minister agrees or disagrees, and with his approval they go into operation; but I may say that so far as I am concerned I have taken, in most instances, the considered recommendation of the Research Council. In some cases I have talked recommendations over with them and they have been withdrawn.
I understand that all the members of the Council do not devote the whole of their time to this work?
No, they do not.
But they convene 4n Ottawa?
How often?
Yes.

As a rule the meetings are held about once a fortnight. The members of the council could not be expected to give their whole time to the work. They are men who have their allotted duties in the universities. They get no salary for this work, but they do give a large amount of time. They
11 p.m. not only attend meetings here but they are more or less at work even when they are absent from Ottawa.

The right hon. gentleman has just read an interesting document, the product of a number of eminent gentlemen, some of whom were biochemists. Now among those "bios" was there a practical fox-breeder-even one practical fox-breeder?

I have read a statement giving the composition of the committee, and that statement also mentions the fact that the foxes were placed in these pens by those who own them in Prince Edward Island. The foxes are kept under the supervision, and subject to the constant observation, of these men who are carrying on the experiment and making the notes. That is the only way in which the investigation could be conducted. Even a practical fox-breeder might not be able to make scientific observation. I do not know how it is with foxes-but generally a successful breeder has the knack of it and has luck-gets along well.

The last observation of the right hon. gentleman is really the one that applies to this industry. The practical and successful breeder does not need the assistance of the "bios" who compose this committee. To quote the language my right hon. friend used in the House a few weeks ago, "honest injun now," does he not think the money is wasted?
I do not.
The right hon. gentleman says he does not?
I do not.
Then may I tell the right hon. gentleman that among the large population in this part of Canada he is an outstanding exception.
That is not always a demerit.

It is very well known that this Council of Industrial and Scientific Research is just a method of providing-well, a sort of pleasant occupation for a number of gentlemen who form little coteries here and there, and to whom the irreverent refer as members of a mutual admiration society. Now just in this connection, a gentleman who is said to be a very eminent man, and whose standing in a university I will not attempt to question, was until lately the head of this Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-I refer to Dr. Macallum. Amongst those who have been born and have lived in Ottawa all their lives, and who are not very easily impressed by the great or the neargreat, there was a very settled conviction that Dr. Macallum was not at all what he was represented to be in connection with this Council of Industrial and Scientific Research. Efforts were made in this
House from time to time to find out what salary Dr. Macallum received in Toronto university before he was transferred to Ottawa but those efforts were unavailing.
Futile.

As my hon. friend from Brome classically says these efforts were futile. But a few short months ago I chanced to read an address by the present president of Toronto University in which he gave the secret away, and he mentioned that Dr. Macallum used to get $4,000 in that institution. He was brought down here and was provided with a position affording much more time for recreation than occupation, and was paid $10,000 a year. So far as I am aware, neither the House nor the country has ever been . given a single proof of any practical work accomplished by Dr. Macallum or this Council of Scientific and Industrial Research. I am not charging the present Government, still less my right hon. friend, with having been the initiators of this method of public expenditure. In times past I recall that other gentlemen, supposed to be very eminent in the scientific world, were also engaged in alleged scientific occupations. To one gentleman we used to vote money annually-indeed, we may do so yet, for I have not scrutinized the Estimates with sufficient care to state definitely-for experiments in electric smelting. From time to time this gentleman interviewed himself and handed out information to the newspapers of wonderful accomplishments at the Soo in connection with electric smelting, but so far as a critical and cynical public ever knew the only thing he turned out were some paper weights. I remember I was favoured with one.
Have you got it yet?

I believe so. I hope to produce it here as Exhibit A to illustrate to the House and to the public what value we received for the expenditure of public money in this way. Now, Dr. Macallum has resigned and no successor has been appointed?
No permanent successor.

Is the $10,000 being
paid to anybody else?
Not at the present time.
Is it to be paid to anybody in the future?
I cannot tell; that will depend on the reorganization.
In any event the work is going on without Dr. Macallum?
Yes.

I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that is the most eloquent commentary that need be made on the value of Dr. Maeallum's services to the country in return for his $10,000 a year. I am not criticising my right hon. friend, in fact, I do not know if his department has had the supervision of this Council from its inception, but; to use his own phrase again: "honest injun, now," isn't it about time we stopped providing for these gentlemen? They are all quite respectable, but none, I submit, renders any service of practical value to this country for the money received. Just take the illustration given to the committee a few minutes ago by my right hon. friend of the expenditure of some $5,000 as a retainer and honorarium, with travelling expenses thrown in, for a gentleman in Toronto to instruct people down in Prince Edward Island in fox-breeding-people who have forgotten more than this gentleman will ever know about foxes. If my right hon. friend requires any information on foxbreeding, all he need do is move down a few seats to the hon. member from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Mclsaac), who will no doubt enlighten him. The report the right hon. gentleman read contains no practical information regarding fox-breeding that was not known before, and much more accurately by the people who are engaged in the industry in Prince Edward Island. All Governments have been sinners in this respect, they have yielded to the importunities of pestering friends, and jobs of this kind have been created for people who have nothing else to do, or who in public competition with practical men could not earn enough for their keep, to use a common phrase. In view of the serious financial situation of the country, I submit to my right hon. friend that he could render no greater national service at the present time than to ask the committee to drop this item.

The suggestion of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) seems to be that Dr. Macallum was furnished with a soft and easy job, to repeat an expression which is sometimes used in the Government service. Yet the strange fact is that Dr. Macallum seems to have voluntarily resigned that job and

gone where his services are appreciated. That would suggest to me that Dr. Macallum is more entitled to commendation than criticism. Without going into details, and particularly without undertaking to sit in' judgment on this foxy business, I wish to say that in regard to some general system for carrying on scientific research in Canada I am cordially with the Government, and I think it is desirable that it should be encouraged. Of course, it should be conducted in a practical way and should be devoted to the development of the natural resources of the country. We have suffered in the past because other countries have given more attention to scientific research than we have. It is a matter of notoriety that much of the success of Germany in industrial affairs was due to scientific research. I have not sufficient knowledge of these matters to go into details, but I do wish to go on record as heartily supporting every effort to employ scientific men to the end that they may devote their talents to the development of the natural resources of Canada. I do hope that if there are any defects in details the criticisms offered today will be taken into consideration, but on the main question of having some well defined system of scientific research I wish to give my cordial support to the action taken by the Government.

Statements have been made that the money voted for the purposes of scientific and industrial research has literally been thrown away. In my judgment, as one who has had something to do with practical affairs, instead of the vote being cut down it should be very materially increased if the . country could possibly afford it. We are lagging behind industrially because we are away behind scientifically. The tremendous waste that is taking place every day could be avoided if we had the leadership of *just such men as Dr. Macallum, to give our industrial leaders the scientific direction which they require. We could pay our national debt out of the waste that is involved in our industries every day. In northern Ontario during the whole period of the war we were importing iron ore from the United States and smelting it into shell when the ore itself only carried thirty per cent of iron. At the same time we were mining ore in northern Ontario, taking it out to the. roasting beds, destroying vegetation, and roasting out of it twenty-three per cent sulphur, then at very great expense putting it through the

smelter and securing only fifty to sixty per cent iron because we have not developed any scientific process to make it possible to separate the precious and coarse metals in the one operation. In those slag heaps there is enough iron to keep every rolling mill in Canada going if we had a process by which the iron could be saved. That is the kind of thing that is going on. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) thinks it is very strange that Dr. Macallum, who was head of the Research Council, should have resigned this fat job that he was holding down, I suppose my hon. friend would consider, as an ornament to society or as the head of a mutual admiration society. Well, why did he resign? Because his worth was recognized by a commercial organization which is willing to give him just double the salary that he was receiving as head of the Research Council.
Does the hon. gentleman state as a fact that Dr. Macallum is now receiving twice the salary he was receiving before?

I am credibly informed that Dr. Macallum has been engaged on a five year contract at $20,000 a year and expenses. I am confident, without having any more than a passing acquaintance with Dr. Macallum, that those who have employed him would not have done so were they not confident that he would earn his salary. But leaving Dr. Macallum out of the question altogether, if this,country is going to advance as it should, we should increase this item rather than decrease it. We should strengthen the hands of the Research Council by giving them a laboratory here in Ottawa where this work can be carried on. I know scores of cases in which men who wanted to get a certain commodity or product analyzed in this country could not do so; they had to go to the United States or to some other country in order to get the information. The committee of the House which dealt with this matter heard the evidence of the heads of the universities, to whom the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) referred, and it was recommended by those gentlemen that a research institute be established and properly equipped with laboratories where research work could be carried on under the most favourable conditions, It will be seen by the evidence given by the heads of the universities before this committee that they do not agree with the view of the member for Brome that this research work should be done in the universities. They say that the business of the men in the universities is to teach what others search out for then and place in their hands, and that if you double up the work- well, the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) shakes his head. But it was the view of all these gentlemen that the man engaged in the teaching profession in the university is not in a position properly to carry on research work. I do not wish to labour the question, but I repeat that instead of reducing this amount we should look forward to increasing it and to giving the Research Council all the necessary facilities for properly carrying out this very important work.

Are the professors to
whom the right hon. gentleman referred in the document which he read-those engaged in the fox farming industry-veterinarians?

The associate
committee which is carrying on the investigation consists of five professors of biochemistry and physiology and two representatives of the Department of Agriculture, one of whom is Dr. Torrance, Veterinary Director General, Health of Animals branch. I should just like to reply briefly to the statements made by my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy). As an exhibition of good-natured banter and persiflage, of its kind, it was excellent; but the very same type of speech has been made on numerous occasions for many years past with reference to scientific men engaged in the work of research. This patient, tireless, exhaustive work does not show itself from day to day, but it frequently results in some discovery, either of synthesis or of analysis, some discovery of the relations of materials and their effects in combination, which puts into the world's productive industries millions upon millions of money and into the economic use of the country products which it otherwise would not have and at lower prices than would otherwise be the case. My hon. friend spoke about Dr. Macallum. I am loath to bring Dr. Macallum's name here; his affairs are his own affairs. But I can tell my hon friend that neither before he took this position nor since has Dr. Macallum been obliged to beg for offers of emolument or for the highest positions. He is at this mement loaned to the Rockefeller Institute, having been selected by them for special work in China during five, six or seven months. Before he was appointed head of the Research Council he received an offer of a position in

With the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) and with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I am in hearty accord as to the desirability of applying science to Canadian industry as rapidly and generally as possible; but neither of these gentlemen told the committee, because neither of them could do so, that any practical result or benefit to Canadian industry has resulted from the work of this Advisory Council of Industrial and Scientific Research.
I just mentioned one.

My right hon. friend
is one of the cheeriest optimists in Canada, and that excellent quality develops and increases as time goes by, and I commend him heartily for it. He mentioned that in a couple of months he expected that so-and-so would likely happen in connection with production of some of the lignite in the West. With him I hope that will be the case. My criticism is not based on any objection to the application of science and industry; quite the reverse; my objection is that real scientists with a practical knowledge of industrial chemistry have not been engaged, and I will give my right hon. friend my authority for saying so. I think the minister, my hon. friend from Algoma and other gentlemen in the House, will not be disposed to question my authority. Having the general knowledge that a person goes through college and university has about* scientific subjects, without having devoted himself to the pursuit of the study of anyone of them in particular, I was anxious to find out from gentlemen competent to speak, what was the practical value to Canadian industry of the work of this Advisory Council. In looking about for the quarter to which I might address my inquiry, it occurred to me that I could not address it to any better informed quarter than to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I, therefore, made inquiry there, and I was told by one of the most

competent officials of that association-and I need not mention either to the minister or to the hon. member for East Algoma that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association makes a specialty of employing competent officials-that while Dr. Macallum might be very eminent as a bio-chemist in a university, he was absolutely useless as an industrial chemist in connection with the industries of this country; that he had absolutely no knowledge on that subject, and the council of which he was a member produced no practical results. The opinion of this official of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association was that no practical results would follow from the work of this Advisory Council of Industrial and Scientific Research until chemists with a knowledge of industrial chemistry were employed in connection with it. That is my reason for the statement that I have made; that is the information I got, and that is the quarter from which I received it. My right hon. friend has described the results that flow from the application of science to industry. My right hon. friend used the phase that it was slow in its processes. In that respect this council measures up to the definition. We in Canada-and in this regard I want to point out that I am in perfect accord with the hon. member for East Algoma- need the application of chemistry and science to Canadian industry; but I desire to see whatever money may be voted for that purpose applied in the proper way, the way to produce results applied, for instance, in connection with those who may be engaged to conduct those scientific inquiries, in securing the services of men who not only have scientific knowledge but are able to apply that knowledge practically. The fact that, according to my informant of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, not one single practical result has so far flowed to Canadian industry from the work of this council, is the strongest possible criticism that may be offered with regard to expenditures of moneys that hava in the past been voted for this purpose. An I said in my opening remarks, I do not offer these observations by way of criticism of the Government, still less of the minister in charge of the Estimates; I am offering them tp the committee as a reason why either this vote should be discontinued or a very different method pursued in future in the expenditure of the money.

As one of those who
some twenty years ago was a student of Dr. Macallum in Toronto University, I
have listened on different occasions in this House to criticisms of that gentleman, and while I should not like to pass upon his ability as a bio-chemist, or on his ability in the position.which he occupied on this Research Council, I should like to say this in justice to him, and I think it is only fair that someone should say it. Twenty years ago Dr. Macallum was one of the few men Canada had ever produced who had an international reputation in science. Dr. Macallum's name was known in every civilized country in the world in which the scientific branch which he taught at Toronto University was studied. I mention that in passing because I think it is only just that should be said about him. .It is an absolute fact that cannot be denied by anybody who knows the subject which he taught to the students in Toronto University. I should like also to say that there have been various investigating committees in England looking into the industrial life of that country and wondering why it was not going ahead as it should have done, particularly since the war, and I have seen reports which stated that one of the main reasons why the industrial life of England was not going ahead was because Germany, for example, went into industrial research work on a much greater scale than England. It was also pointed out that all these industrial research committees in Germany were working for the advancement of that country, and that many large industries there had these research committees working for them. They would often find that a man or a hody would be engaged on investigations for a number of years before accomplishing any result which would be of use to the industry, hut then after many years work results would be attained which would be very beneficial to the industry and fully justify the length of time that had been taken up by the investigation. The Industrial Research Council of Canada has been in existence for only a short time, and I think we should wait with patience for a while at least to give them an opportunity to bring forth results which I believe will be of great benefit to the Dominion of Canada. I believe personally that a research council of some kind should) be maintained to a reasonable extent, I think it is one of the most needed requirements of this country at the present time.

I do not wish to
detain the committee at any lenght, but I desire to say just a few words in reply to

the observations made by the hon. member for East Algoma. I would hardly agree with him in his statement that the university is not the proper place for research.
That was not my statement, but the statement of the presidents of the universities and the professors in the universities, made to a committee of this House.

I was just going to take that up. I could hardly imagine that the Principal of McGill University made any such statement. My recollection is that this committee sat within a year. Prior to that the Principal of McGill had been laid aside by a paralytic stroke, and his successor was only appointed within ~the last few months. At any rate, if the president did make such a statement I cannot agree with him. I think the whole history of research is contrary to that statement. If we take McGill University for instance, we find among the scientific discoverers who have shone in Canada in recent years, such men as Professor Rutherford, who was a professor at McGill, Professor Nicholson, also of McGill, Sir William Dawson, a principal of McGill, and one of the greatest discoverers in geology that we ever had, and Professor Barnes who was one of the great discoverers of the action of freezing water and eminent in scientific research along that line. Then if we go to the Old Land we remember that the great surgical discoverer, Lord Lister, was a professor at Glasgow if I mistake not, that the discoverer of chloroform, Sir James Simpson, was a professor at Edinburgh, and that Lord Kelvin was a professor at Glasgow. If we look at the history of scientific research in Great Britain and Canada we shall find that a large proportion of the most eminent men were college professors. My hon. friend from East Algoma made the statement that a man could not be an investigator on research work and be a professor at the same time. I hardly think that is correct. But I would have him and the House remember that a university has advanced students, such as the students of the graduate school of Johns Hopkins University, probably the greatest school for research in the whole of North America. I am, however, opposed to the idea of incurring expense for laboratories, which would be expensive to maintain, here in Ottawa. These laboratories should be at the universities, where the best work, in my humble opinion, can

be done. I would not like the hon. member for East Algoma or any other hon. member of the House to think for a moment that I am opposed to the application of s'cience to industry. We are all in favour of it. It is simply a question of what is the best way to arrive at the desired end.
I should like to inquire what formalities have to be complied with in order to obtain the services of the Research Council.

If my hon. friend wants information with reference to any particular scientific research problem, just make application to the Chairman of the Council. If in the operation of an industry he comes up against a difficulty which puzzles- him, an exact statement of his problem should be sent tc the Research Council. It would then be taken into consideration, and if they thought it was of sufficient importance to work out, they would hand it over to some person who was au fait in that particular line of research, and through a bursary or fellowship he could be given the means to defray his expenses while he was at work on that problem. That, however, cannot be thoroughly and efficiently done without a central laboratory, and we shall have a discussion on that in the future.

Is it the intention of the Government to take advantage of the Advisory Research Council for furthering investigation into the electrical treatment of titaniferous iron ores? The Government some years ago spent quite a large sum of money studying the treatment in electrical furnaces of these titaniferous ores, and if I remember rightly, they sent Dr. Stansfield of McGill University to Sweden and Norway and other countries to investigate the processes in vogue there. I understood from the report of Dr. Stansfield that titaniferous iron ores could be successfully treated in Canada provided we could get electrical power cheap enough, but that the development of the electric furnace had to be carried still further before any economic advantage could be taken of our deposits. Has the minister -any information as to the activities of the board in that respect? If not, is it the intention of the Government to investigate this matter further with a view to utilizing our deposits?

If I mistake not, the laboratory which is carried on by the

Mines Department has had that subject before it and has conducted research with reference to it. Does my hon. friend remember to whom Dr. Stansfield made his report?
To the Mines Department.

Well, I am quite certain that the Advisory Council has not undertaken any ambitious work in that respect. It is a pretty costly undertaking, and I suppose they have not felt themselves in a position to do anything in that direction.	*

I do not think the experiment would be extremely costly in view of the developments which have been made in the electrical furnace. There is only the question of the magnetic selection of ores after they have been crushed, so that the iron ore might be obtained and the titani-ferous portion be so reduced as to be economically treated afterwards in the electrical furnace. I think this would be of great interest to the province whence I come, because we have there in large quantities deposits of titaniferous ores, and also of oriferous and iron ores. In the county of Charlevoix there are deposits which were exploited about forty or fifty years ago, but operations had to be discontinued owing to the economic difficulties that had to be contended with. They could not compete with iron ores free from titaniferous alloy. I think the Advisory Council would find that it is not so expensive to complete the investigations already carried on under the direction of the Mines Department by Dr. Stansfield. I do not think very much study of the subject is necessary.
I will bring the matter to the attention of the council.

Item agreed to.
Inspection and Sale Act, administration of, $2,500.
What is it that is inspected?
Hides, leather, etc.; the payment is chiefly by fees.
Are there any grants in this?
This is all for the principal inspector.
Are any of the officials in connection with this matter paid any fees?

This is the
salary of Elzear Cote, who is the inspector of hides for Quebec. It also includes expenses in connection with the inspection of hides and the supervising of binder twine, $250, stationery and printing, $130. The salary of Cote is $1,620.

Item agreed to.
International Customs Tariffs' Bureau, $1,400.
What is this?

This is larger than the vote of last year because during the war, for two years, no appropriation was made. The work went on, not as efficiently as before, but still it was continued. This is an added appropriation to cover expenses. We pay a certain proportion, about $600 a year, as our share.

On page 105 of the
Estimates, I find an item for a similar proposition. I would call the attention of the minister to item No. 12, which is similar to this item. Will be explain the reason for these items appearing under two different heads in the Estimates? The item on page 105 is:
Chief, Foreign Tariff's Division.

That is an entirely different thing. This is a fee that we pay to the International Customs arrangement which gathers together the tariffs of all the different countries and keeps track of their changes, distributing the information to the associate nations. We are one of the associate countries and we pay this $600 a year as our contribution towards the maintenance of this arrangement.

The information given
me the other night in regard to the other item is practically the same as the statement now made by the minister.
It was an explanation along similar lines. We have to keep a staff here for the collation of that information and its distribution to our own people.
Who determines Canada's contribution?
A certain sum is necessary for carrying on this work, and it is divided as fairly as possible among the associate nations. The amount is only small.

According to the Auditor General's report, Canada has not paid anything for six years. At page Z-30 I find the following item:
International Customs Tariffs Bureau-Canada's share of cost for six years to March 31, 1920, $3,972.
Apparently the department has to wait quite a long while to ascertain what its share is to the general fund.
The information I have here is just as I have given it. However, I will look into what my hon. friend has said:

Item agreed to.
West India Cable, $38,933.33.

This is the
customary vote under the contract. The contract is one entered into between the British Government, ourselves, and the West Indian colonies. Its purpose was to extend cable connection between the various West India Islands and to provide for a reduction in the tolls charged for the service. The British Government pays the same amount as we do. The contract has two years yet to run. The different West Indian governments pay proportionally. The service was considered necessary, and as we were interested in it we contribute towards the subsidy.

Is it paid to the
Cable Company?
Yes.
When was the service established?

About six or
seven years ago.
What' is the real purpose of the service? Is it for commercial purposes only or for news and general purposes?

It is for commercial purposes and for the sending of any messages that anyone wants to send; it is not a newspaper service. It represents about four thousand miles which is served by the companies which are subsidized.
Is this regarded as a subsidy to the cable companies?

Yes.
<Sir George Foster.]

Item agreed to.
Printing of Parliamentary and Departmental publications, including cost of translation $125,000.	'
[

This is a new vote as it appears here and is following out the resolution of Parliament which, instead of paying for the printing done by departments, now asks that the departments pay for their own printing, Parliament paying what is necessary for its own purposes. All the departments come under the resolution referred to, which I consider a very salutary one. The departments formerly acted under the belief that Parliament would pay the whole of their printing bills, and were probably less careful in the matter of printing. The new policy throws the cost of printing upon the department which is responsible for it.

Each department will
have its own printing done?
Yes.

Is the cost of the new
distribution service that the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell) used to conduct from here included in this vote?
The news service for the hon. member for Durham?
The news service formerly conducted by the ex-President of the Privy Council?

There is no
news service by the hon. member for Durham.
I am glad to know the minister acknowledges that it did exist.
I do not know what my hon. friend is referring to.
I would like to know of the cost of the Canadian Record, which used to be published under the ex-President of the Privy Council, is included in this item?

No, nothing of the kind. This covers departmental printing done by the Trade and Commerce Department entirely, and that department undertakes no news service such
12 m. as was carried on formerly by the Publicity Department conducted under the President of the Privy Council.

Is there any news service
carried on at present?
I cannot speak as to what is being carried on under the President of the Privy Council, but I am of the opinion that the news service such as we formerly had is now a thing of the past.

' I believe last year all the Government printing was done through a certain department which controlled the distribution of the material that every department had to print. May I ask the minister if this change means that the minister himself will have charge of the distribution of the material for printing?

There is no
change made at all in the distribution itself. This simply applies to the bill for the printing.

At the Printing
Bureau?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
